analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed whether the COVID-19 pandemic altered routine early childhood vaccination uptake in Scotland, motivated by observed changes in family working patterns and increased vaccine focus during the pandemic.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational cohort study used linked administrative health data for Scotland to examine population-based individual-level records of children reaching 12 or 24 months of age between January 2019 and December 2021 (N = 199,574 children).
analysis.methods: Timely uptake of six routine vaccinations was assessed using logistic regression to compare pandemic and pre-pandemic cohorts, with adjustment for sociodemographic variables and interaction analysis across area deprivation, parental socioeconomic class, urban-rural residence, and maternal ethnic group.
analysis.main_results: Vaccination uptake either remained stable or increased for five of the six vaccines during the pandemic, and most interaction terms were not statistically significant, indicating broadly similar effects across sociodemographic groups.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as evidence of resilience in Scotland’s childhood immunisation programme during the pandemic, while noting that large pre-existing inequalities persisted across socioeconomic and ethnic groups.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that routine early childhood vaccination programmes can maintain coverage during public health emergencies, but targeted strategies are needed to address structural barriers and reduce persistent inequalities.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s observational design and reliance on administrative data limit causal inference, and while the large sample size strengthens precision, unmeasured confounding and generalisability to other settings remain concerns.

analysis.summary_en: This population-based cohort study in Scotland evaluated whether the COVID-19 pandemic affected early childhood vaccination uptake by comparing pandemic and pre-pandemic cohorts using linked administrative health data for 199,574 children. Uptake remained stable or increased for five of six vaccines during the pandemic, with no significant sociodemographic interactions, indicating broadly uniform effects. However, large pre-existing inequalities persisted, particularly by area deprivation and maternal ethnic group. The authors conclude that Scotland’s immunisation programme showed resilience during the pandemic but highlight the need for safeguarding early-life vaccines and addressing structural barriers. The study’s observational design and administrative data limit causal inference, though the large sample size supports precision.

papers.abstract_zh: 目标:COVID-19 大流行改变了许多家庭的工作模式,并导致人们更加关注 疫苗。这可能影响了儿童早期对 疫苗接种 的吸收。我们利用苏格兰的关联行政健康数据来调查该流行病是否与幼儿 疫苗接种 的吸收变化有关。研究设计:回顾性观察 队列研究 设计检查苏格兰基于人口的个人层面关联的行政健康数据。方法:我们评估了六种常规 疫苗接种 - 6 合 1 疫苗、肺炎球菌结合物 疫苗 (PCV)、轮状病毒 疫苗、Hib/MenC 疫苗、麻疹、腮腺炎和风疹 (MMR) 的及时摄取情况疫苗 和 PCV 加强剂 - 在苏格兰 12 个月或 24 个月大的儿童中,2019 年 1 月至 2021 年 12 月(N = 199,574 名儿童)。逻辑回归模型评估了大流行病 队列研究 与大流行前 队列研究 的吸收情况,并对关键社会人口统计学变量进行了调整和不调整。交互分析评估了关联是否因地区贫困、父母社会经济阶层、城乡居住地和母亲种族群体而异。结果:在大流行期间,六个 疫苗 中的五个的 疫苗接种 吸收率要么保持稳定,要么有所增加。大多数相互作用在统计上并不显着,这表明流行病对不同社会人口群体的影响大致相似。然而,在大流行期间,先前存在的巨大不平等现象仍然存在,最贫困地区和管理/专业家庭的接受程度较高,而一些少数民族群体的接受程度较低。结论:苏格兰的儿童免疫计划在大流行期间表现出弹性,但先前存在的不平等现象仍然存在。未来的规划应包括保护早期生命 疫苗 和解决结构性障碍。

papers.title: Broad permissiveness of mammalian nectin-4 orthologs for morbilliviruses: a notable exception in dolphin nectin-4
papers.abstract: Morbilliviruses utilize signalling lymphocytic activation molecule (SLAM) and nectin-4 as their major cellular receptors and exhibit distinct host specificities despite sharing common receptor usage. While species-specific differences in SLAM have been extensively investigated, the contribution of nectin-4 to morbillivirus host range remains poorly understood because nectin-4 is highly conserved among mammals. Here, we systematically compared the receptor activities of nectin-4 orthologs from human, dolphin, bat, dog and seal for representative morbilliviruses, including measles virus (MV), cetacean morbillivirus (CeMV), canine distemper virus (CDV), phocine distemper virus (PDV) and Myotis bat morbillivirus (MBaMV). Cell–cell fusion, virus infection and plaque assays demonstrated that most nectin-4 orthologs efficiently supported infection by all tested viruses. In contrast, dolphin nectin-4 exhibited markedly reduced receptor activity for MV, PDV and MBaMV, while remaining fully functional for CeMV and CDV. This phenotype was consistently observed with multiple clinical MV isolates. Mutational analyses identified amino acid residue 63 as a key determinant of this receptor specificity. Substitution of glutamic acid at position 63 in dolphin nectin-4 with glycine restored MV receptor activity to a level comparable to that of human nectin-4. These findings demonstrate that nectin-4 is generally a broadly permissive morbillivirus receptor but that specific amino acid differences can substantially influence receptor usage. elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 麻疹病毒利用 SLAM 和 nectin-4 作为主要受体,但由于 nectin-4 在哺乳动物中的高度保守性,宿主 的特异性仍然知之甚少。本研究旨在探讨 nectin-4 在确定麻疹病毒 宿主 范围中的作用,重点关注 麻疹病毒。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究系统地比较了来自人类、海豚、蝙蝠、狗和海豹的nectin-4直系同源物对代表性麻疹病毒的受体活性,包括麻疹病毒、鲸类麻疹病毒、犬瘟热病毒、福辛瘟热病毒和鼠耳蝠麻疹病毒。

elements_zh.main_results: 大多数 nectin-4 直系同源物有效支持所有测试的麻疹病毒(包括 麻疹病毒)的感染。Dolphin nectin-4 对 麻疹病毒、海狗瘟热病毒和鼠耳蝠麻疹病毒的受体活性显着降低,但对鲸豚麻疹病毒和犬瘟热病毒仍具有完全功能。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,nectin-4 通常是麻疹病毒广泛允许的受体,但特定氨基酸差异可显着影响受体的使用,突出了 宿主 系列和跨物种 传播 中受体兼容性的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果提供了对 麻疹病毒 宿主 特异性的分子机制的见解,并可能为了解病毒 传播 和制定有针对性的干预措施提供策略。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅基于摘要证据,虽然它确定了关键的氨基酸差异,但需要进一步的实验验证来确认这些发现的功能含义。由于分析范围有限,证据强度中等。

papers.title: Prevalence and factors associated with immunization non-completion among children aged 12–23 months at Kisoro General Hospital, Uganda: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Immunization non-completion, defined here as a child missing at least one age-appropriate vaccine dose under Uganda’s national immunization schedule (UNEPI), remains a critical public health problem in sub-Saharan Africa, exposing children to preventable diseases. In Uganda, coverage falls substantially below the WHO target of 90%, particularly in rural districts. This study determined the prevalence of immunization non-completion among children aged 12–23 months at Kisoro General Hospital and identified associated socio-economic and healthcare-related factors. A cross-sectional study was conducted from October to December 2024 at Kisoro General Hospital among 275 caregivers of children aged 12–23 months attending the immunization clinic, selected by systematic random sampling. Immunization non-completion was defined as failure to receive at least one age-appropriate dose per the UNEPI schedule (BCG, OPV, pentavalent, PCV, rotavirus, measles, and yellow fever vaccines) by 12–23 months of age. Data were collected via structured, pre-tested questionnaires and verified immunization card records. Descriptive statistics, bivariate chi-square tests, and multivariable logistic regression were performed using Stata version 15.1 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). The participation rate was 90.5% (275/304). Caregivers who declined participation ( n = 10), were excluded after consent due to absent immunization records ( n = 12), or whose children fell outside the 12–23-month age range ( n = 7) are reported in full in the Results section. The prevalence of immunization non-completion was 34.2% (94/275; 95% CI: 28.5–39.8%). In multivariable analysis, significant predictors included lack of formal caregiver education (aOR = 3.3, 95% CI: 0.93–11.49; p = 0.044), delayed initiation of immunization beyond three weeks of birth (aOR = 7.3, 95% CI: 3.66–14.72; p < 0.001), unfriendly health worker attitude (aOR = 5.8, 95% CI: 1.29–11.46; p = 0.022), and vaccine stock-outs (aOR = 6.1, 95% CI: 1.71–14.67; p = 0.005). Children of caregivers aged 25–34 years were less likely to have incomplete immunization than those of caregivers aged over 34 years (aOR = 0.3, 95% CI: 0.16–0.76; p = 0.008). One in three children attending Kisoro General Hospital had incomplete immunization, far below national and global targets. Modifiable determinants at both caregiver and health system levels were identified. Targeted interventions including caregiver education, timely postnatal vaccination, health worker training, and vaccine supply strengthening are urgently needed.

papers.abstract_original: Immunization non-completion, defined here as a child missing at least one age-appropriate vaccine dose under Uganda’s national immunization schedule (UNEPI), remains a critical public health problem in sub-Saharan Africa, exposing children to preventable diseases. In Uganda, coverage falls substantially below the WHO target of 90%, particularly in rural districts. This study determined the prevalence of immunization non-completion among children aged 12–23 months at Kisoro General Hospital and identified associated socio-economic and healthcare-related factors. A cross-sectional study was conducted from October to December 2024 at Kisoro General Hospital among 275 caregivers of children aged 12–23 months attending the immunization clinic, selected by systematic random sampling. Immunization non-completion was defined as failure to receive at least one age-appropriate dose per the UNEPI schedule (BCG, OPV, pentavalent, PCV, rotavirus, measles, and yellow fever vaccines) by 12–23 months of age. Data were collected via structured, pre-tested questionnaires and verified immunization card records. Descriptive statistics, bivariate chi-square tests, and multivariable logistic regression were performed using Stata version 15.1 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). The participation rate was 90.5% (275/304). Caregivers who declined participation ( n = 10), were excluded after consent due to absent immunization records ( n = 12), or whose children fell outside the 12–23-month age range ( n = 7) are reported in full in the Results section. The prevalence of immunization non-completion was 34.2% (94/275; 95% CI: 28.5–39.8%). In multivariable analysis, significant predictors included lack of formal caregiver education (aOR = 3.3, 95% CI: 0.93–11.49; p = 0.044), delayed initiation of immunization beyond three weeks of birth (aOR = 7.3, 95% CI: 3.66–14.72; p < 0.001), unfriendly health worker attitude (aOR = 5.8, 95% CI: 1.29–11.46; p = 0.022), and vaccine stock-outs (aOR = 6.1, 95% CI: 1.71–14.67; p = 0.005). Children of caregivers aged 25–34 years were less likely to have incomplete immunization than those of caregivers aged over 34 years (aOR = 0.3, 95% CI: 0.16–0.76; p = 0.008). One in three children attending Kisoro General Hospital had incomplete immunization, far below national and global targets. Modifiable determinants at both caregiver and health system levels were identified. Targeted interventions including caregiver education, timely postnatal vaccination, health worker training, and vaccine supply strengthening are urgently needed.

news.content: measles Introduction & Top Questions Transmission and symptoms Treatment and complications Measles vaccine and eradication efforts Similar illnesses References & Edit History Quick Facts & Related Topics Images, Videos & Interactives At a Glance measles summary Measles An infant with skin rash characteristic of measles. measles disease Also known as: rubeola Written and fact-checked by Britannica Editors Encyclopaedia Britannica's editors oversee subject areas in which they have extensive knowledge, whether from years of experience gained by working on that content or via study for an advanced degree.... Britannica Editors Last updated Aug. 11, 2026 • History Top Questions What is measles? Measles is a highly contagious viral disease, a hallmark symptom of which is a blotchy rash. It is most common in children and can be prevented through vaccination. What happens if you get measles? If you get measles, you are likely to develop a high fever , cough , and runny nose and have red, watery eyes. These symptoms are followed by a characteristic rash that spreads from the face downward. Symptoms appear 7–14 days after exposure and can lead to severe complications, including pneumonia , encephalitis ( brain inflammation ), diarrhea , or death, particularly in people who are unvaccinated. Can you get measles if you had a vaccine? It is possible, though rare, to get measles even after being vaccinated. Such breakthrough infections occur because the MMR vaccine , which protects against measles, is about 97 percent effective after two doses. However, vaccinated individuals who become infected usually experience a milder illness and are less likely to spread it to others, providing crucial protection for vulnerable populations, including the very young and the elderly. Why is measles coming back? Measles is resurging primarily due to declining vaccination rates, which have dropped below the 95 percent threshold required for herd immunity . Increased vaccine hesitancy and interruptions in routine immunization schedules, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic , have been major contributing factors to this decline. Because the measles virus is highly contagious, it spreads easily and quickly through under-vaccinated communities. What is the recommended treatment for measles? No drug is effective against measles. The only treatment required is control of fever, rest in bed, protection of the eyes, care of the bowels, and sometimes steam inhalations to relieve irritation of the bronchial tree. When no complications occur, the illness lasts 10 days. What are complications of measles? Measles complications are frequent and include superimposed bacterial ear infection, pneumonia, and lung infection. The virus can also cause hepatitis, appendicitis, and gangrene of the extremities. Encephalitis is a rare occurrence. Deaths attributed to measles usually result from secondary bronchopneumonia caused by bacterial organisms entering the inflamed bronchial tree. Can measles affect adults? Measles is most common in children but may appear in older persons who escaped it earlier in life. Immunity to measles following an attack is usually lifelong. Is there a vaccine for measles? Measles vaccines are live vaccines that work against measles alone or in combination with other agents, specifically with rubella (MR), mumps and rubella (MMR), or mumps, rubella, and varicella (MMRV). The vaccines are typically given in two doses, the first before 15 months of age and the second dose later; timing of the dosages varies by country or region. News • Correction: Trump-Vaccines story • Aug. 11, 2026, 10:09 AM ET (AP) measles , contagious viral disease marked by fever , cough , conjunctivitis , and a characteristic rash. Measles is most common in children but may appear in older persons who escaped it earlier in life. Infants are immune up to four or five months of age if the mother has had the disease . Immunity to measles following an attack is usually lifelong. The disease can be prevented through immunization with the MMR vaccine . Learn more in this list of vaccine-preventable diseases . Transmission and symptoms Measles Giant cell in a patient with measles. Measles is so highly communicable that the slightest contact with an active case may infect a susceptible person. After an incubation period of about 10 days, the patient develops fever, redness and watering of the eyes, profuse nasal discharge , and congestion of the mucous membrane s of the nose and throat—symptoms often mistaken for those of a severe cold. This period of invasion lasts for 48 to 96 hours. The fever increases with appearance of a blotchy rash , and the temperature may rise as high as 40 °C (about 105 °F) when the rash reaches its maximum. Twenty-four to 36 hours before the rash develops, there appear in the mucous membranes of the mouth typical maculae, called Koplik spots —bluish white specks surrounded by bright red areas about 1 / 32 inch (0.75 mm) in diameter. After a day or two the rash becomes a deeper red and gradually fades, the temperature drops rapidly, and the catarrhal symptoms disappear. Britannica Quiz A Visit with the Word Doctor: Medical Vocabulary Quiz Treatment and complications No drug is effective against measles. The only treatment required is control of fever, rest in bed, protection of the eyes, care of the bowels, and sometimes steam inhalations to relieve irritation of the bronchial tree. When no complications occur, the illness lasts 10 days. Although uncomplicated measles is seldom fatal, infection with the virus has been shown to induce a form of “immune amnesia,” whereby measles virus eliminates as many as half of the antibodies generated against other infectious agents to which an individual was exposed previously. Thus, persons who survive measles infection may become vulnerable once again to a range of other diseases, such as chickenpox and polio . By contrast, individuals vaccinated against measles do not experience a loss of immunity to other infectious agents. Deaths attributed to measles usually result from secondary bronchopneumonia caused by bacterial organisms entering the inflamed bronchial tree. Complications of measles are frequent and include a superimposed bacterial ear infection or pneumonia or a primary measles lung infection. Encephalitis is a rare occurrence. Measles virus can invade various organ systems and cause hepatitis , appendicitis , and gangrene of the extremities. A large percentage of cases of severe measles are associated with inadequate intake of vitamin A , and there is evidence that treatment with vitamin A may reduce measles complications. On very rare occasions, persistent infection with a mutant measles virus can cause a degenerative central nervous system disease called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), in which there is a gradual onset of progressive behavioral and intellectual deterioration. Motor incoordination and impairment of speech and sight subsequently develop. The final stages of stupor, dementia, blindness, and death occur within six to nine months. There is no treatment for SSPE. Measles vaccine and eradication efforts How We Develop New Vaccines Worried about diphtheria? No? Thank vaccines. See all videos for this article Mortality caused by measles declined steadily in the 20th century as the health of children and infants improved and effective treatment of complications became possible through the use of sulfonamide and antibiotic drugs. The widespread use of measles vaccine , beginning in the late 1960s, raised hopes for the eventual eradication of the disease. In the following decades, however, measles remained a leading cause of childhood mortality worldwide, primarily because attack rates remained high in less-developed countries, where factors such as malnutrition and weak public health infrastructure challenged infant health and the establishment of immunization programs. In the early 21st century, campaigns were initiated to increase vaccination , particularly in less-developed countries. International efforts led to a significant reduction in measles cases and deaths, bringing global elimination of the disease within reach. At the same time, supporting this progress, many wealthier countries, including the United States and some countries in the European Union , had successfully eradicated measles. Explore Britannica Premium! The trusted destination for professionals, college students, and lifelong learners. SUBSCRIBE In the second decade of the 21st century, however, large measles outbreaks continued to occur in countries with low vaccination rates. In late 2019 in Samoa , for instance, a severe outbreak of measles resulted in school closures and government shutdown, followed by a mass vaccination campaign to prevent further spread of the disease. Measles also reemerged in several countries where it previously had been eradicated, a trend attributed to alarming declines in vaccination coverage. Of particular concern was the return of measles in developed countries such as the United States, where the disease had been eliminated by 2000, and the United Kingdom. In these countries, measles reemerged in the form of small outbreaks that were typically concentrated in areas with relatively high proportions of unvaccinated individuals. In early 2025, the death of a child amid a measles outbreak in Texas marked the country’s first death caused by measles in more than a decade. Coincident with the return of measles in more developed countries, however, was a massive surge in the disease in countries with traditionally low vaccination coverage, resulting in large increases in measles cases worldwide. Global incidence was notably high in 2019, with more than 364,800 cases reported between June and July alone that year—far exceeding the number of cases reported worldwide over that time frame for any year since 2006, according to officials with the World Health Organization (WHO). The largest increases occurred in countries in Africa, Europe, and the Western Pacific. By early 2020 the Democratic Republic of the Congo was in the midst of a severe measles epidemic , with more than 6,000 deaths according to WHO. WHO and health officials in regions affected by measles outbreaks increased efforts to bolster vaccination rates to stop the disease from spreading further. Find out from Dr. Tina Tan of Northwestern University why adult vaccination against various types of diseases is important Learn about the importance of adult vaccination against measles and other diseases. See all videos for this article Measles vaccines are live vaccines that work against measles alone or in combination against other agents, specifically with rubella ( MR ), mumps and rubella ( MMR ), or mumps, rubella, and varicella ( MMRV ). The vaccines typically are given in two doses. In the United States, for example, the first dose is given at 12 to 15 months of age, and the second dose is recommended at four to six years. In other countries, the vaccine is given first at nine months and the second dose later. The second dose of MMR must be given at least four weeks after the first dose; in adults whose vaccination status is uncertain, the two doses typically are given four weeks apart. The youngest age at which the vaccines can be given is six months, though revaccination (with two doses) is needed later. See MMR vaccine . Also called: rubeola Key People: Maurice Hilleman Guillaume de Baillou Related Topics: Koplik spot MMRV vaccine Morbillivirus MR vaccine subacute sclerosing panencephalitis See all related content Similar illnesses Measles must be differentiated from other disorders accompanied by an eruption. In roseola infantum , a disease seen in babies, a measleslike rash appears after the child has had a high temperature for two or three days, but there is no fever at the time of the rash. German measles ( rubella ) can be superficially differentiated from measles by the shorter course of the disease and mildness of the symptoms. Sometimes the rashes of scarlet fever , serum reactions, and other conditions may, on certain parts of the body, look like measles. Drugs that may produce rashes similar to measles are phenobarbital, diphenylhydantoin, the sulfonamides, phenolphthalein, and penicillin . Britannica Editors Last updated Aug. 11, 2026 • History Top Questions What is measles? Measles is a highly contagious viral disease, a hallmark symptom of which is a blotchy rash. It is most common in children and can be prevented through vaccination. What happens if you get measles? If you get measles, you are likely to develop a high fever , cough , and runny nose and have red, watery eyes. These symptoms are followed by a characteristic rash that spreads from the face downward. Symptoms appear 7–14 days after exposure and can lead to severe complications, including pneumonia , encephalitis ( brain inflammation ), diarrhea , or death, particularly in people who are unvaccinated. Can you get measles if you had a vaccine? It is possible, though rare, to get measles even after being vaccinated. Such breakthrough infections occur because the MMR vaccine , which protects against measles, is about 97 percent effective after two doses. However, vaccinated individuals who become infected usually experience a milder illness and are less likely to spread it to others, providing crucial protection for vulnerable populations, including the very young and the elderly. Why is measles coming back? Measles is resurging primarily due to declining vaccination rates, which have dropped below the 95 percent threshold required for herd immunity . Increased vaccine hesitancy and interruptions in routine immunization schedules, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic , have been major contributing factors to this decline. Because the measles virus is highly contagious, it spreads easily and quickly through under-vaccinated communities. What is the recommended treatment for measles? No drug is effective against measles. The only treatment required is control of fever, rest in bed, protection of the eyes, care of the bowels, and sometimes steam inhalations to relieve irritation of the bronchial tree. When no complications occur, the illness lasts 10 days. What are complications of measles? Measles complications are frequent and include superimposed bacterial ear infection, pneumonia, and lung infection. The virus can also cause hepatitis, appendicitis, and gangrene of the extremities. Encephalitis is a rare occurrence. Deaths attributed to measles usually result from secondary bronchopneumonia caused by bacterial organisms entering the inflamed bronchial tree. Can measles affect adults? Measles is most common in children but may appear in older persons who escaped it earlier in life. Immunity to measles following an attack is usually lifelong. Is there a vaccine for measles? Measles vaccines are live vaccines that work against measles alone or in combination with other agents, specifically with rubella (MR), mumps and rubella (MMR), or mumps, rubella, and varicella (MMRV). The vaccines are typically given in two doses, the first before 15 months of age and the second dose later; timing of the dosages varies by country or region. News • Correction: Trump-Vaccines story • Aug. 11, 2026, 10:09 AM ET (AP) measles , contagious viral disease marked by fever , cough , conjunctivitis , and a characteristic rash. Measles is most common in children but may appear in older persons who escaped it earlier in life. Infants are immune up to four or five months of age if the mother has had the disease . Immunity to measles following an attack is usually lifelong. The disease can be prevented through immunization with the MMR vaccine . Learn more in this list of vaccine-preventable diseases . Transmission and symptoms Measles Giant cell in a patient with measles. Measles is so highly communicable that the slightest contact with an active case may infect a susceptible person. After an incubation period of about 10 days, the patient develops fever, redness and watering of the eyes, profuse nasal discharge , and congestion of the mucous membrane s of the nose and throat—symptoms often mistaken for those of a severe cold. This period of invasion lasts for 48 to 96 hours. The fever increases with appearance of a blotchy rash , and the temperature may rise as high as 40 °C (about 105 °F) when the rash reaches its maximum. Twenty-four to 36 hours before the rash develops, there appear in the mucous membranes of the mouth typical maculae, called Koplik spots —bluish white specks surrounded by bright red areas about 1 / 32 inch (0.75 mm) in diameter. After a day or two the rash becomes a deeper red and gradually fades, the temperature drops rapidly, and the catarrhal symptoms disappear. Britannica Quiz A Visit with the Word Doctor: Medical Vocabulary Quiz Treatment and complications No drug is effective against measles. The only treatment required is control of fever, rest in bed, protection of the eyes, care of the bowels, and sometimes steam inhalations to relieve irritation of the bronchial tree. When no complications occur, the illness lasts 10 days. Although uncomplicated measles is seldom fatal, infection with the virus has been shown to induce a form of “immune amnesia,” whereby measles virus eliminates as many as half of the antibodies generated against other infectious agents to which an individual was exposed previously. Thus, persons who survive measles infection may become vulnerable once again to a range of other diseases, such as chickenpox and polio . By contrast, individuals vaccinated against measles do not experience a loss of immunity to other infectious agents. Deaths attributed to measles usually result from secondary bronchopneumonia caused by bacterial organisms entering the inflamed bronchial tree. Complications of measles are frequent and include a superimposed bacterial ear infection or pneumonia or a primary measles lung infection. Encephalitis is a rare occurrence. Measles virus can invade various organ systems and cause hepatitis , appendicitis , and gangrene of the extremities. A large percentage of cases of severe measles are associated with inadequate intake of vitamin A , and there is evidence that treatment with vitamin A may reduce measles complications. On very rare occasions, persistent infection with a mutant measles virus can cause a degenerative central nervous system disease called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), in which there is a gradual onset of progressive behavioral and intellectual deterioration. Motor incoordination and impairment of speech and sight subsequently develop. The final stages of stupor, dementia, blindness, and death occur within six to nine months. There is no treatment for SSPE. Measles vaccine and eradication efforts How We Develop New Vaccines Worried about diphtheria? No? Thank vaccines. See all videos for this article Mortality caused by measles declined steadily in the 20th century as the health of children and infants improved and effective treatment of complications became possible through the use of sulfonamide and antibiotic drugs. The widespread use of measles vaccine , beginning in the late 1960s, raised hopes for the eventual eradication of the disease. In the following decades, however, measles remained a leading cause of childhood mortality worldwide, primarily because attack rates remained high in less-developed countries, where factors such as malnutrition and weak public health infrastructure challenged infant health and the establishment of immunization programs. In the early 21st century, campaigns were initiated to increase vaccination , particularly in less-developed countries. International efforts led to a significant reduction in measles cases and deaths, bringing global elimination of the disease within reach. At the same time, supporting this progress, many wealthier countries, including the United States and some countries in the European Union , had successfully eradicated measles. SUBSCRIBE In the second decade of the 21st century, however, large measles outbreaks continued to occur in countries with low vaccination rates. In late 2019 in Samoa , for instance, a severe outbreak of measles resulted in school closures and government shutdown, followed by a mass vaccination campaign to prevent further spread of the disease. Measles also reemerged in several countries where it previously had been eradicated, a trend attributed to alarming declines in vaccination coverage. Of particular concern was the return of measles in developed countries such as the United States, where the disease had been eliminated by 2000, and the United Kingdom. In these countries, measles reemerged in the form of small outbreaks that were typically concentrated in areas with relatively high proportions of unvaccinated individuals. In early 2025, the death of a child amid a measles outbreak in Texas marked the country’s first death caused by measles in more than a decade. Coincident with the return of measles in more developed countries, however, was a massive surge in the disease in countries with traditionally low vaccination coverage, resulting in large increases in measles cases worldwide. Global incidence was notably high in 2019, with more than 364,800 cases reported between June and July alone that year—far exceeding the number of cases reported worldwide over that time frame for any year since 2006, according to officials with the World Health Organization (WHO). The largest increases occurred in countries in Africa, Europe, and the Western Pacific. By early 2020 the Democratic Republic of the Congo was in the midst of a severe measles epidemic , with more than 6,000 deaths according to WHO. WHO and health officials in regions affected by measles outbreaks increased efforts to bolster vaccination rates to stop the disease from spreading further. The vaccines typically are given in two doses. In the United States, for example, the first dose is given at 12 to 15 months of age, and the second dose is recommended at four to six years. In other countries, the vaccine is given first at nine months and the second dose later. The second dose of MMR must be given at least four weeks after the first dose; in adults whose vaccination status is uncertain, the two doses typically are given four weeks apart. The youngest age at which the vaccines can be given is six months, though revaccination (with two doses) is needed later. See MMR vaccine . news.content: The United States has broken another record. Unfortunately, this is not one anyone should celebrate. As of July 23, 2026, the CDC had confirmed 2,318 cases of measles in the United States. That is already more than the 2,289 cases reported during all of 2025, with more than five months still remaining in the year. Measles outbreaks are back with a vengeance! This is the largest number of measles cases the country has recorded in 35 years. The last time the total was higher was 1991, when 9,643 cases were reported. That was nine years before the United States declared measles eliminated. The obvious question is: How did this country resurrect a disease it had already defeated? Measles Outbreaks Set a 35-Year Record The latest CDC numbers are sobering: - 2,318 confirmed measles cases in 2026 - 35 newly reported outbreaks - 45 jurisdictions reporting cases - 151 hospitalizations - 93 percent of cases linked to outbreaks - 93 percent of patients unvaccinated or of unknown vaccination status - 69 percent of patients younger than 20 Nearly half of all cases have occurred among children and teenagers between 5 and 19 years old. Another 20 percent have involved children under 5. There have been no reported measles deaths in the United States so far this year. That is welcome news, but it should not be interpreted to mean the disease is harmless. Three Americans died from measles in 2025, including two previously healthy children. Of this year’s 456 patients under age 5, 45 have required hospitalization. Among adults with measles, approximately one in ten has been hospitalized. How Accurate if the FDA’s Measles Count? Do you trust the CDC? There have been substantial staff cuts. This is partially a political issue because anything associated with vaccination these days is political. We suspect that the measles outbreaks, as dramatic as they seem, are undercounting actual cases. Families may not seek medical attention for a child who is sick. Then, usually seven to ten years later, persistent measles virus in the brain can trigger progressive neurological deterioration. The immune system normally remembers bacteria and viruses it has encountered before. That memory helps the body respond more rapidly the next time a familiar germ appears. Measles can destroy some of those memory cells. After the rash and fever disappear, a child may look completely recovered. But the immune system can remain less capable of recognizing other infectious threats for months or even years. That means the damage from measles may extend beyond the measles infection itself. A child could become more susceptible to influenza, pneumonia or other illnesses that the immune system previously knew how to fight. It is almost as though measles breaks into the immune system’s library and tears pages out of its reference books. If one person with measles enters a room containing ten susceptible people, as many as nine may become infected. The virus spreads through the air when someone breathes, coughs or sneezes. Viral particles can remain suspended for as long as two hours after the infected person has left. People can also spread measles before they realize they are sick. A medical resident or emergency physician may have studied measles in a textbook but never encountered it in an exam room. A child with fever and cough may spend hours in a crowded waiting room before the rash is recognized. By then, patients, parents, nurses, receptionists and other staff members may have been exposed. That is why anyone who suspects measles should call the doctor, urgent-care center or emergency department before arriving. Once measles is suspected, the patient should be masked and isolated immediately. Clinicians should contact the local health department and collect samples for laboratory confirmation. A disease can become unfamiliar without becoming harmless. In fact, forgetting what measles looks like gives this extraordinarily contagious virus one more opportunity to spread. The Actual Price of Measles You could easily be paying for measles. Researchers at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health reviewed the cost of responding to measles outbreaks in 18 states. They estimated an average cost of approximately $43,000 for every measles case, although the figure ranged from under $7,000 to more than $243,000. Those estimates include medical care and public-health work such as laboratory testing, vaccination clinics, contact tracing and emergency response. For many years, those imported infections usually fizzled out. The virus encountered too few susceptible people to keep spreading. That protective barrier is now developing big cracks. That may sound like a small decline, but measles is so contagious that communities generally need vaccination rates around 95 percent to prevent sustained transmission. The national average also conceals large local pockets where vaccination rates are much lower. Once measles reaches one of those communities, an imported case can become an outbreak. The risk from the vaccine may begin to feel more immediate than the disease it prevents. Eventually, vaccine coverage declines enough for the disease to return. Then everyone is reminded why the vaccine was developed in the first place. Are Immigrants Responsible for Measles Outbreaks? Whenever we report on measles, some readers blame immigrants. Measles certainly can enter the country through international travel. But the southern border has been closed for more than a year. And yet cases have climbed to unprecedented levels this year. The overwhelming majority of patients have been U.S. residents. The large wave of infections in 2025 began in Texas and New Mexico. Investigators traced many early cases to a tight-knit Mennonite community in West Texas, where vaccination rates were low. Similar patterns have been observed in some Amish and ultra-Orthodox Jewish communities, as well as certain other religious or cultural groups where vaccination is discouraged. Vaccine hesitancy has also grown in parts of the broader population where distrust of public health institutions has increased. Tourists can bring measles into the US and Americans who vacation, work or study abroad can also bring measles back with them. A wall cannot stop an airborne virus carried home by an American tourist. Does the MMR Vaccine Work to Stop Measles Outbreaks? news.content: News Sports Life Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH At least 6 kids sickened by measles in Delaware as outbreak grows Isabel Hughes Delaware News Journal Aug. 12, 2026, 6:56 a.m. ET Measles cases in Delaware have reached double digits, with 20 people in the state testing positive for the highly-contagious virus as of Aug. 11. The majority of cases − 13 − are in residents age 20 and older, according to the Delaware Division of Public Health. One case was reported in a Delawarean between 10 and 19 years old, while the remaining six cases were in children 9 and under. All confirmed cases are in Kent County. Delaware's outbreak comes as measles cases continue to rise nationwide. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the number of U.S. cases reported in 2026 has already surpassed the total reported in all of 2025. Here's what to know about measles. What are measles? Measles is a highly contagious, acute viral illness that begins with early symptoms of fever, cough, runny nose and conjunctivitis (pink eye), lasting two to four days before rash onset. The rash typically occurs three to five days after symptoms begin and usually appears on the face and spreads down the body. Measles can cause severe health complications, including pneumonia, brain inflammation and death. The virus is transmitted by direct contact with infectious droplets or by airborne spread when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The measles virus can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Infected people are contagious from four days before the rash starts through four days after rash development. The incubation period for measles from exposure to fever is usually about 10 days, with a range of seven to 12 days. And from exposure to rash onset is usually about 14 days with a seven to 21-day range.More: Back‐to‐school vaccines: what DE requires before school year starts How do you treat measles? There is no specific antiviral cure for the measles. However, if you haven't been previously vaccinated against the measles, you can still be vaccinated to head off the worst symptoms, if you act fast enough. "If people older than six months of age are exposed to measles and are not immune by previous illness or vaccination, they can get a measles vaccine for up to three days after contact with the virus," advised the Mayo Clinic. "After the vaccine you don't need to stay home, also called quarantine." Antibodies can also be given for up to six days after exposure, though they are prioritized for people who cannot get the measles vaccine, such as infants younger than 6 months old, pregnant women, severely immunocompromised people or people who have other medical contraindications to vaccination, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Who should be most worried about measles? Jennifer Horney, professor and chair of the University of Delaware's Department of Epidemiology, said she believes the biggest concern should be parents of children who can't be vaccinated yet. "That's one of the things that people who make decisions not to vaccinate don't understand − is that you're making a decision for a lot of people (by not vaccinating)," she said. How contagious is measles? Per Horney, each person who is infected will likely spread to about 18 susceptible people. "So, if we compare that to something like COVID or flu that we're more familiar with, you would typically spread to maybe two susceptible people," Horney said. "If someone is on your plane and they have measles, if you're not vaccinated, you are going to get measles. It just is very, very effective at spreading, and you can spread before you have the rash." Who is most at risk during a measles outbreak? People who are unvaccinated, pregnant, immunocompromised or too young to be vaccinated face the highest risk of severe complications, DPH said. The first dose for infants is usually given between 12 and 15 months. Anyone who cannot get the vaccine but who has come into contact with someone suspected to have measles should immediately contact their primary care provider or Delaware's Office of Infectious Disease Epidemiology at (302) 744-4990 for guidance. Given the Delaware measles outbreak, can my infant get an early dose of the MMR vaccine? Speak to your pediatrician. Babies six months and older are physically able to receive the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, though an early dose − defined as before 12 months of age − won't count toward their regular vaccine schedule, which is typically two doses. The second dose is generally given to kids between 4 and 6 years of age. Are adults who were vaccinated decades ago still protected? If you were born before 1957, you are considered immune. If you were fully vaccinated, you’re also considered immune. If you’re concerned, however, your doctor can order a blood test to check for immunity. Such testing is fairly common. Why are measles on the rise in the United States? The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to the CDC. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated and most people are protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventives, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. USA TODAY contributed to this report. news.content_title: Ohio measles outbreak cases rise again, surpass last year's numbers
news.content: Akron mayor addresses firing of officer, settlement with Tucker estate News Sports Entertainment Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE Ohio measles outbreak cases rise again, surpass last year's numbers Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Aug. 13, 2026, 3:17 p.m. ET Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues to grow, spreading to another county and surpassing the total number of cases from 2025 at the last count. Harrison County Public Health reported a measles case there on Aug. 12. Statewide, the Ohio Department of Health is reporting 69 cases in 11 counties, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Aug. 13. That's up from 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Nationwide, measles cases nationwide hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released July 22 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 2,295 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio; counties reporting cases Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashtabula: 17 Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 7 Geauga: 16 Harrison: 3 Holmes: 2 Knox: 1 Ottawa: 1 Trumbull: 2 Tuscarawas: 8 Wayne: 2 Unknown: 7 The latest case count reflects two previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with 45 in 2025, seven cases in 2024 and one case in 2023. Where are measles cases spreading? While Harrison County Public Health reported one case of measles as of Aug. 7, the state dashboard shows two additional cases there. The Wayne County Health Department reports some of its cases are likely associated with a previously identified measles exposure event at Smokey Lane Stables, 686 Smokey Lane Road NW in Sugarcreek, on July 17. One of the Tuscarawas cases is from the same event, that health department reports. Geauga Public Health reports that the individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. In Trumbull County, health officials report that infected individuals were at the Walmart in Liberty on July 29 and Akron Children's Mahoning Valley Emergency Department in Boardman on Aug. 2, during the time they were able to spread the virus. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Why are measles cases on the rise? Ohio vaccination rates Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventives, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine ahead of back-to-school season. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023, the most recent year available from ODH. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, USA TODAY reports. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. analysis.time: Published 2026-08-13; event ongoing through August 2026 with case counts updated to August 7, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Ohio, USA; 11 counties (Ashtabula, Cuyahoga, Franklin, Geauga, Harrison, Holmes, Knox, Ottawa, Trumbull, Tuscarawas, Wayne); affected age range 15 months to 20 years; exposures linked to public venues including Smokey Lane Stables (Sugarcreek), Bloomfield Horse Sale/Livestock Auction, Walmart (Liberty), and Akron Children's Mahoning Valley Emergency Department.
analysis.event: Third measles outbreak of 2026 in Ohio, reported by local and state health departments; confirmed cases rising and surpassing 2025 totals; Ohio Department of Health (ODH) and county health departments are investigating and reporting exposures.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 69 confirmed cases statewide across 11 counties as of August 7, 2026; up from 45 cases in 10 counties on August 1; 2,295 measles cases reported nationwide in 2026, the highest since 1991; risk emphasized for unvaccinated children and adults, immunocompromised individuals, pregnant women, and those under 5 or over 20 years; measles is highly contagious with airborne transmission and can cause severe complications including pneumonia and encephalitis.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: ODH and county health departments are conducting case investigations, contact tracing, and public exposure notifications; vaccination campaigns are being emphasized by ODH Director Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff; statewide MMR coverage for children and adolescents was 91.5% in 2023, below herd immunity threshold; uncertainty remains regarding further spread and vaccination uptake; no deaths reported in Ohio cases as of the evidence.

analysis.brief_en: Ohio’s third measles outbreak of 2026 continues to expand, with state health officials reporting 69 confirmed cases across 11 counties as of August 7—surpassing the 45 cases recorded in 2025. The outbreak spans communities from Ashtabula to Wayne, with exposures linked to public venues including livestock auctions and retail locations. Nationally, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, with 2,295 infections reported so far in 2026, driven by declining vaccination rates that have eroded herd immunity. Ohio’s MMR coverage for children and adolescents stood at 91.5% in 2023, below the 95% threshold needed to prevent sustained spread. Health authorities are urging vaccination, noting that two doses of MMR are 97% effective, while warning that measles can cause severe complications including pneumonia and encephalitis, particularly in young children and immunocompromised individuals.

news.content: News Sports Packers Business Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals NEWS Wisconsin measles outbreak grows to 15 confirmed cases, 6 probable Measles spreading in southwestern Wisconsin Sarah Volpenhein Milwaukee Journal Sentinel Aug. 13, 2026Updated Aug. 14, 2026, 12:41 p.m. CT A measles outbreak in southwestern Wisconsin has grown to 15 confirmed and six probable cases. Health officials believe there is active local transmission and more cases likely exist in the community. The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles year in decades, with nearly 2,500 cases recorded so far in 2026. Most of those infected in the Wisconsin outbreak were unvaccinated children or teens. An additional 13 cases of measles have been confirmed in Iowa County in southwestern Wisconsin, along with six probable cases, fueling an outbreak state health officials warn may still be spreading. The latest cases, reported on Aug. 13, bring the total number of outbreak cases to 15 confirmed and six probable, but health officials suspect more people may be infected. Two cases of measles were identified earlier this week in Iowa County and neighboring Lafayette County, and both people were believed to have been exposed in Wisconsin. "The rapid emergence of these cases, particularly among people who have not traveled outside of Wisconsin, indicates that there is active local transmission," said Ryan Westergaard, chief medical officer and state epidemiologist for communicable diseases for the Wisconsin Department of Health Services. "It is very likely that additional cases exist in the community that have not yet been identified or reported to public health," he said during a call with reporters Aug. 13. No public locations have been identified where people may have been exposed, Westergaard said. No hospitalizations related to the outbreak have been reported. U.S. dealing with worst measles year in decades The U.S. is dealing with its worst measles year in decades. The country has recorded nearly 2,600 measles cases so far in 2026, the most of any year since 1991, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The outbreaks come as vaccination rates are slipping. More than 90% of people who have contracted the highly contagious virus were either unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status. In Wisconsin, all but one of this year's cases were unvaccinated, according to the state measles dashboard. Wisconsin's last outbreak occurred in 2025 when the state recorded 36 measles cases in Oconto County. Local health officials managed to contain that outbreak before it ballooned out of control. Other states have endured months-long outbreaks with cases climbing into the hundreds. An ongoing outbreak in Utah that has infected 715 people first began in June 2025. In Wisconsin, local health officials are interviewing people with confirmed cases to identify close contacts. They are reaching out directly to those who may have been exposed to ask about their vaccination status and symptoms, Westergaard said. "We are hoping that this is a small outbreak, and that we contain it quickly," he said. "Right now, it’s a dynamic situation." Measles symptoms typically start a week to two weeks after infection with a high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A few days after the first symptoms arise, red spots or bumps appear on the face and near the hairline. That rash will spread to the rest of the body. People may also get tiny white spots inside the mouth a few days after symptoms begin. Immunization rates falling amid vaccine skepticism The latest cases in Wisconsin come as children prepare to head back to school this month and in September. Wisconsin kindergartners have one of the lowest vaccination rates in the country against measles, and the percentage of children getting the shot has fallen over the last decade, amid increasing skepticism of routine childhood vaccinations. Only about four of every five toddlers in Wisconsin have received the first dose of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, which is highly effective at preventing illness, according to state data. Most of Wisconsin's latest cases are among children under 18 years old, according to the state Department of Health Services. And nationally, children or teens make up two-thirds of all measles infections this year, according to the CDC. Under President Donald Trump's administration, federal health officials have pushed to upend the nation's long-established childhood vaccine schedule. On Aug. 10, Trump signed an executive order calling for children to receive fewer vaccines and suggesting splitting some vaccines − including the one for measles, mumps and rubella − into multiple shots. The executive order is only a recommendation because states − not the federal government − set vaccination requirements for schools, childcare centers and other settings. Still, the American Academy of Pediatrics called the move "unscientific and dangerous," especially as measles cases reach a 35-year high. Top health officials in Wisconsin also took aim at the executive order, saying it contradicted the best available science on vaccines and disease prevention. "There is no new scientific evidence that justifies changing recommendations that have, and continue to, protect children across the United States," state Department of Health Services Secretary-designee Kirsten Johnson said in a statement issued Aug. 13. This story has been updated to add new information. Reporter Madeline Heim, of the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, contributed to this report. Georgia State researchers say yes August 11, 2026 2:23 PM By: Sofi Gratas Share this page Share this page on Twitter Share this page on Facebook Share this page on Email Share this page on Print republish Primary Content play pause Listen Listening... 00:00 / 01:02 LISTEN: While not a replacement for the measles vaccine, an oral antiviral developed at Georgia State University could be an option for more vaccine-hesitant populations. GPB's Sofi Gratas explains. Caption False claims about vaccines such as the measles/mumps/rubella vaccine (above) have led to growing public mistrust in the disease-preventing measure. Credit: Adobe Stock The data is clear: Far fewer people, specifically children, are getting vaccinated against infectious diseases now than in the past. False claims about vaccines have led to growing public mistrust. And when these claims are amplified by public health officials, there are measurable results. Researchers out of Georgia State University are considering additional ways to prevent disease spread, by testing out an antiviral against measles-like diseases. To effectively test a potential antiviral treatment for measles, there would need to be clinical trials on humans. Microbiologist Richard Plemper and his team at Georgia State have instead tested on a cousin of the measles virus: canine distemper. The research, published in the science magazine Nature Microbiology, is funded by the National Institutes of Health. “We want to be able to have a drug that people can take at home — make the hurdle as low as possible,” Plemper said. They tested the oral antiviral pre- and post-exposure to the virus on ferrets. The key was to look at not whether the animals were exposed to the virus, which is inevitable, but if their immune systems recognized the pathogen and responded. In the pre-clinical trials, Plemper’s team found little to no detectable antibodies in the animals' immune systems. "We can completely prevent any disease in the contacts," Plemper said. "So complete success." If an antiviral were developed for human measles, it would not be a replacement for the measles vaccine, which is the most effective way to prevent disease. But Plemper says it could be a good option for people who are vaccine-hesitant, especially as the U.S. is on track to lose its measles elimination status. "Where we are now, we feel there is a need to augment vaccination, but with a pharmacological option," Plemper said. Uptake would still ultimately be up to the public. This fall, the Pan American Health Organization will review epidemiological evidence on measles outbreaks in the U.S. and decide whether the country has retained or lost its elimination status, held since 2000. There were more cases of measles this year — case counts currently stand at 2,465 — than in any other year in the past two decades. Georgia has largely been spared, with only five reported measles cases this year so far. That’s still double last year’s case count. She joined GPB in June 2022 as a Report for America Corps member. Her focus is on the crisis facing rural communities that consistently rank near the bottom nationwide in health and health care. Sofi is a 2020 graduate of the University of Georgia's Grady School of Journalism. Prior to joining GPB, she worked at the Red and Black and WUGA. Kennedy Jr. Add Topic Record U.S. measles outbreak: What Tennessee families should know before school starts Afton Pratt Knoxville News Sentinel Aug. 10, 2026, 3:06 p.m. ET Hear this story A little over halfway through the year, the number of confirmed measles cases has reached a record high. As of Aug. 6, there were 2,465 cases, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The number of cases has surpassed 2025 totals and is the highest recorded in 35 years. Children under 5 years old are among the age groups most at risk of contracting measles. With school starting for the 2026-27 academic year, including pre-K and kindergarten, there are steps parents can take to reduce their children's risk of contracting the virus. The disease was declared eliminated in 2000, but as vaccination rates decline, measles cases are on the rise, according to Reuters. U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. recently said he believes children should be vaccinated against measles despite his vaccine skepticism. Measles outbreaks have been reported in nearby Virginia and other Eastern states, including Pennsylvania. Nearly half of all U.S. cases have been recorded among people ages 5 to 19. With the back-to-school season on the horizon, here's what Tennessee residents should know about measles. What are the measles? The measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads through the coughing and sneezing of an infected person. Measles can live in the air for up to two hours after a person who has the virus leaves the area and anyone unprotected who comes into contact with the air or surface is at risk, according to the CDC. In order to be fully protected against the measles, the CDC says a person needs two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccines. Children can get the first dose between 12 and 15 months old. The second dose can be administered between ages four and six, according to the CDC. Measles symptoms usually begin seven to 14 days after exposure. Here's what to look out for: A high fever that can spike to over 104°F. A cough and runny nose. Red and watery eyes, or pink eye. Red and blotchy rash. There is no antiviral treatment for the measles. It is recommended those who contract the disease and are not protected get the vaccine up to three days after contact with the measles or receive an antibody shot than can help ease the infection and lower the risk of complications, according to the Mayo Clinic. Drinking water and resting are also recommended to help with the measles. Measles cases in Tennessee Although there is a rise in measles cases nationwide, Tennessee has seen only a few measles cases so far in 2026. As of Aug. 7, there have only been three measles cases this year, two were in Middle Tennessee and the third case was recorded in Shelby County, according to the Tennessee Department of Health. In 2025 there were eight confirmed measles cases in the state. With the return to school, parents might feel anxiety surrounding the decline in the measles, mumps and rubella vaccination rates, however the vaccination rate in Tennessee is above the national average, according to Johns Hopkins University. The most recent data shows that 94% of kindergartners received measles immunizations in the 2024-25 school year, the target is 95% and the national average is 93%. Tennessee was still down in vaccination rates compared to previous years. Tennessee allows religious exemptions for vaccinations, non-medical exemptions are sometimes linked to increased disease transmission, according to Johns Hopkins. Tennessee's non-medical vaccine exemption rate is lower than the national average. The TDH recommends isolating at home and calling your healthcare provider if you have suspicions that you have been exposed to the measles, especially if you are unvaccinated. Afton Pratt covers trending news for The Knoxville News Sentinel and Tennessee. She can be reached at ampratt@usatodayco.com. Featured Weekly Ad

analysis.event: A reported record-high measles outbreak in the U.S. in 2026, with Tennessee-specific guidance issued as schools prepare to reopen for the 2026–27 academic year.

Post-exposure prophylaxis (vaccine within 3 days or antibody shot) may reduce infection severity.

Tennessee has recorded three measles cases so far in 2026, up from eight in 2025, though the state’s kindergarten vaccination rate (94%) remains above the national average. Health authorities emphasize the importance of two MMR vaccine doses for protection, as measles spreads easily through airborne droplets and surfaces, with no antiviral treatment available. Tennessee’s Department of Health urges isolation and medical consultation for suspected exposures, particularly among unvaccinated individuals, while noting that religious exemptions exist but are lower than the national average.

news.content: Skip to main content HOME NEWS Politics & Government Work & the Economy Education Election 2026 Environment Civil Rights Commentary ABOUT SUBSCRIBE DONATE Part of States Newsroom Search Search Politics & Government Work & the Economy Education Election 2026 Environment Civil Rights 3:30 News Story Health Care Measles outbreak in Southwest Wisconsin grows; most taken ill weren’t vaccinated By Erik Gunn - August 14, 2026 3:30 am Wisconsin's top doctor says a new outbreak shows measles is spreading in the state. (Photo by Getty Images Plus) A report earlier this week of a couple of measles cases in Southwest Wisconsin has turned into an outbreak, with 13 more confirmed cases and six probable cases of the viral illness, the state health department reported Thursday. The outbreak, in Iowa and Lafayette counties, highlights the importance of getting vaccinated for measles, considered the safest and most effective way to prevent the spread of the virus, said Dr. Ryan Westergaard, the chief medical officer in the communicable disease bureau of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services. Ryan Westergaard, M.D., Wisconsin Dept. of Health Services The new group of measles patients who have been diagnosed are in Iowa County, Westergaard told reporters at a DHS briefing on the findings. Most of them were not vaccinated for measles, he said. DHS announced two measles cases Tuesday, one in Iowa County and one in Lafayette County, that were confirmed through tests at the Wisconsin State Lab of Hygiene. Those were the third and fourth measles cases in Wisconsin in 2026, and were not related to the first two this year, which were linked to out-of-state travel. Subsequent investigation by the local public health departments in the two counties turned up the 13 confirmed and six suspected cases that DHS announced Thursday. None of the current cases have been tied to travel. “The rapid emergence of these cases, particularly among people who have not traveled outside of Wisconsin, indicates that there is active local transmission, and it’s very likely that additional cases exist in the community that have not yet been identified or reported to public health,” Westergaard said. State tracks 23 cases so far Westergaard said DHS would not release the ages or age range for any of the people with confirmed measles cases in the current outbreak in order to protect their privacy. The department maintains a state registry for all measles cases that includes age ranges and vaccination status. Thursday evening, that record showed that of the 23 confirmed or suspected cases identified in Wisconsin in 2026, three were in children age 4 or younger, 11 were in children ages 5 to 17, and nine were in adults ages 18 or older. Westergaard said that it’s likely that there are more people with measles whose cases haven’t been identified and therefore aren’t on the state’s dashboard. With one exception, the patients identified in 2026 were not vaccinated for the measles virus, according to DHS. One has been hospitalized. Vaccine is ‘single best tool’ to stop outbreaks DHS is asking people to verify whether they’ve had the MMR vaccine — the shot that includes protection against measles, mumps and rubella. That information is probably available from a person’s regular health provider, if they have one, or from the Wisconsin immunization registry. The MMR vaccine is usually given in a two-shot sequence: the first dose when a child is 12 to 15 months old, and the second when the child is 4 to 6 years old. “Having received two doses of MMR vaccine provides exceptional, long-lasting protection, and this vaccine remains our single best tool to stop this and future outbreaks,” Westergaard said. For an adult without a record of the shot or who is uncertain about having had it, it is safe to get an additional shot, he said. DHS is also asking people to be familiar with measles symptoms. Westergaard said those include a high fever, a red rash that starts at the head and spreads down and covers the whole body, a cough, a runny nose and red or bloodshot eyes. A person who develops those symptoms, or whose family member experiences them, should call their regular healthcare provider, Westergaard said. People with the symptoms should call ahead before visiting a clinic, urgent care or the emergency room, he said, so that medical personnel can take precautions to prevent airborne spread of the virus before a patient arrives to protect other patients in the facility’s waiting room. Easily spread virus “Measles is known to be one of the most contagious viruses,” Westergaard said, “and we treat every case very seriously, because our goal is to completely stop measles transmission in the community anytime we have a case or a cluster of cases.” Measles can cause serious health problems, according to DHS — pneumonia, deafness, and brain damage as a result of swelling from the disease. Local public health agencies in the two counties haven’t identified specific public places where the virus might have spread, Westergaard said. One of the jobs of local public health departments is to track contagious illnesses such as measles in their communities or counties, he said. DHS supports local agencies as they work to trace who else has been exposed to the virus. Trump urges shift in childhood vaccine recommendations, calls for splitting up MMR vaccine When a person who’s been exposed has been identified, they’re monitored for symptoms “to make sure that if any new cases pop up, we can get them isolated right away,” Westergaard said. While the current outbreak is still small, “it’s a dynamic situation,” he added. With help from DHS, local health departments are tracing the spread of the virus and watching for more people who develop symptoms, “because that would be a sign that it’s getting larger.” New Trump order ‘contradicts the best available science’ Thursday’s announcement follows an order Monday from President Donald Trump. Wisconsin’s top health official said Thursday that Trump’s order goes against the best scientific recommendations for measles prevention. Trump’s order calls for separating the MMR vaccine into separate shots for each illness. “There is no new scientific evidence that justifies changing recommendations that have, and continue to, protect children across the United States,” said Kirsten Johnson, secretary-designee of Wisconsin DHS, in a statement released Thursday. “The executive order does not square at all with our recommendations on how to prevent measles or other vaccine-preventable diseases,” Westergaard said. “It was not science-based. It actually contradicts the best available science about how to prevent disease and keep kids healthy.” DHS early this year turned from the Trump administration’s Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s vaccine recommendations after the agency cast aside previous longstanding vaccine guidance. DHS instead has endorsed the childhood vaccine recommendations from the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Family Physicians. Westergaard said vaccinations in Wisconsin have fallen below the 95% rate that helps ensure widespread protection from illnesses that vaccines can prevent, and are even below 90%. That has happened for many complex reasons, he said — including misinformation, sometimes spread deliberately. Wisconsin has so far avoided the “massive outbreaks” of measles that have occurred in states such as Utah, Texas and North Carolina, Westergaard said. Public health officials can contain the illness if they learn early of cases and are able to move quickly to identify and quarantine patients. But that’s more challenging because the state’s vaccination rate is lower than it should be, he said. In addition to encouraging more vaccination, cooperation with public health measures is “a second layer of defense,” Westergaard said. “Let’s work together as a community, as a team, when an outbreak happens — be willing to share information, be willing to stay home when any symptoms happen, and allow us to identify the extent of an outbreak and to stop it.”
