analysis.time: Published 2026-08-14; event period spans August 2026 with active local transmission reported on August 14.
analysis.location_and_population: Southwest Wisconsin, specifically Iowa and Lafayette counties; affected population includes children (4 or younger, 5–17 years) and adults (18+ years); no ages released for current cases to protect privacy.
analysis.event: A measles outbreak with confirmed and probable cases reported by the Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) on August 14, 2026; DHS officials confirmed active local transmission and warned of likely undetected cases; event is ongoing and under investigation.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 23 total cases (13 confirmed, 6 probable, plus 4 earlier travel-linked cases); one hospitalization; 95% of identified patients were unvaccinated; risk of severe outcomes including pneumonia, deafness, and brain damage; measles is highly contagious; vaccination coverage in Wisconsin below 95% target.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: DHS and local health departments are tracing exposures, monitoring contacts, and isolating cases; public urged to verify MMR vaccination status via providers or Wisconsin immunization registry; DHS endorses CDC-aligned recommendations from AAP and AAFP; officials warn of potential for larger outbreak due to low vaccination rates; uncertainty remains about undetected cases and specific exposure sites.

analysis.brief_en: A measles outbreak in Southwest Wisconsin has grown to 23 cases, including 13 confirmed and six probable, with most patients unvaccinated, state health officials reported on August 14, 2026. The outbreak, centered in Iowa and Lafayette counties, marks the first locally acquired transmission in Wisconsin this year, with no travel links. One person has been hospitalized, and officials warn measles poses risks of severe complications such as pneumonia and brain damage. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services is coordinating with local agencies to trace contacts and isolate cases, while urging residents to verify their MMR vaccination status. Health authorities attribute the outbreak to declining vaccination rates below the 95% threshold needed for community protection and condemned a recent federal order to split the MMR vaccine as unsupported by science.

news.content: US CDC records more than 2,500 measles cases so far in 2026 Updated Fri, August 14, 2026 at 2:56 PM UTC Aug 14 (Reuters) - The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said on Friday there were 2,566 confirmed measles cases in the country so far this year, expanding the highest annual total in more than 35 years. Here are some details: • The overall 2026 figures represent the highest number of U.S. cases in a single year since a major resurgence of the highly contagious disease in the period from 1989 to 1991, with more than 55,000 infections and 123 deaths. • Measles-related hospitalizations this year stand at 169 so far with zero deaths, compared to 243 hospitalizations and three deaths in 2025. • As many as 93% of this year's cases were in unvaccinated individuals or people whose vaccination status was unknown, with the rest having received one or two doses of vaccine before being infected, the CDC said. • Infections were documented by the CDC this year in 45 states along with New York City and the District of Columbia. There have been 38 new outbreaks reported in 2026, compared to 48 in 2025. • A South Carolina outbreak had sickened nearly 1,000 people over six months after it began in October 2025 to become the largest single-location U.S. outbreak since measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000. • A surge in measles cases during the past two years has coincided with a steady slump in MMR immunization rates for children since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. (Reporting by Christy Santhosh in Bengaluru; Editing by Anil D'Silva)

Here are some details: • The overall 2026 figures represent the highest number of U.S. cases in a single year since a major resurgence of the highly contagious disease in the period from 1989 to 1991, with more than 55,000 infections and 123 deaths. • Measles-related hospitalizations this year stand at 169 so far with zero deaths, compared to 243 hospitalizations and three deaths in 2025. • As many as 93% of this year's cases were in unvaccinated individuals or people whose vaccination status was unknown, with the rest having received one or two doses of vaccine before being infected, the CDC said. • Infections were documented by the CDC this year in 45 states along with New York City and the District of Columbia. There have been 38 new outbreaks reported in 2026, compared to 48 in 2025. • A South Carolina outbreak had sickened nearly 1,000 people over six months after it began in October 2025 to become the largest single-location U.S. outbreak since measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000. • A surge in measles cases during the past two years has coincided with a steady slump in MMR immunization rates for children since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. (Reporting by Christy Santhosh in Bengaluru; Editing by Anil D'Silva)

Reynolds Listen 0:00 / 4:34 Key Takeaways Federal prosecutors tied a 37‐month prison term and $1,457,898 forfeiture to laundering Medicare fraud proceeds for a Russia-linked criminal network. Fraud operations leveraged nominee-owned DME companies and falsified corporate documentation to route Medicare reimbursements through U.S. accounts into shells and foreign banks. Community oncology care showed adjusted median overall survival of 46 vs 29 months in metastatic breast cancer and 12 vs 6 months in metastatic NSCLC versus SEER. Higher treatment initiation rates at independent practices likely contributed materially to observed survival advantages, including across subtypes with recent therapeutic innovation. Cryo-EM epitope mapping revealed protective anti-measles immunity extends beyond H protein, with F-targeting 4F09 suppressing viremia to undetectable levels in infected rats. SHOW MORE The top news stories in medicine today. Advertisement Morning Medical Update © batuhan toker - stock.adobe.com New York man sentenced for laundering Medicare fraud proceeds for Russian criminal organization Elnar Zarbailov was arrested in 2024 as he attempted to flee to Azerbaijan. A Staten Island man has been sentenced to 37 months in prison for laundering nearly $1.5 million in Medicare fraud proceeds on behalf of a transnational criminal organization based in Russia, as part of what the Department of Justice (DOJ) has called the largest health care fraud case it has ever prosecuted. Related content: Unmasking $14.6B in health care fraud: Inside the DOJ's largest-ever health care takedown Elnar Zarbailov, 42, a dual U.S.-Azerbaijani citizen, served as a fixer and money launderer for the organization, which used fraudulent durable medical equipment (DME) companies, fronted by nominee owners armed with false corporate documents, to deposit Medicare reimbursement checks into U.S. bank accounts and funnel the money to shell companies and overseas banks. Zarbailov deposited fraud proceeds from five DME companies and transferred funds to accounts including those located abroad. He was arrested at JFK Airport in September 2024 as he attempted to board a flight to Azerbaijan and pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering in October 2025. In addition to his prison sentence, he was ordered to forfeit $1,457,898. Community oncology practices match or beat national survival benchmarks for two major cancers A new study found better or comparable overall survival for metastatic breast cancer and lung cancer patients treated at independent community oncology practices. Patients with metastatic breast cancer and metastatic non-small cell lung cancer treated at community oncology practices had overall survival rates that were consistently better than or comparable to national population benchmarks, according to a new study from the Community Oncology Alliance (COA) analyzed using the Flatiron Health Research Database (FHRD). After adjusting for age, sex, race and cancer subtype, median overall survival for metastatic breast cancer patients at community practices was 46 months, compared with 29 months in the national Surveillance, Epidemiology and End Results (SEER) database; for metastatic non-small cell lung cancer, the figures were 12 months versus 6 months. Researchers found that higher rates of treatment initiation at community practices likely drove a significant portion of the survival advantage, particularly for breast cancer subtypes where major therapeutic advances have occurred in recent years. The study, funded by the Community Oncology Alliance with support from BioNTech, Gilead, Johnson & Johnson and Pfizer, adds to a growing body of evidence that independent community practices deliver high-quality care to a patient population that includes historically underserved groups. Scientists map first comprehensive set of human antibodies against measles virus One antibody reduced measles virus levels in infected animals to undetectable levels, pointing toward a potential treatment for those who cannot be vaccinated. National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded researchers have isolated and mapped the first comprehensive group of human antibodies targeting the measles virus, laying the groundwork for a potential measles treatment at a time when cases are rising in the U.S. and globally, according to a study published in Cell Host & Microbe. The team, led by Erica Ollmann Saphire, Ph.D., MBA, of the La Jolla Institute for Immunology, engineered more than 100 individual human monoclonal antibodies from a vaccinated donor and used cryo-electron microscopy to produce the first atomic-resolution maps of human antibodies bound to measles virus proteins. The findings upend a long-held assumption that protection against measles is driven almost entirely by antibodies targeting the virus's H protein; the study found that antibodies against the F protein can also confer powerful, independent protection. One F protein antibody, designated 4F09, was the most protective in the study, reducing measles virus levels in infected rats to undetectable levels by locking the protein in place and preventing the virus from entering human cells. No approved measles treatment currently exists in the U.S., leaving immunocompromised patients, pregnant women, and infants too young to be vaccinated without options. More than 470,000 measles cases were reported globally in 2024, and the U.S. has seen at least 72 outbreaks since January 2025. analysis.time: Published on 2026-08-10; event date not explicitly reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: United States; research conducted by U.S.-based institutions (La Jolla Institute for Immunology, NIH-funded team).
analysis.event: Scientists isolated and mapped the first comprehensive set of human antibodies targeting the measles virus, identifying an antibody (4F09) that reduced measles virus levels to undetectable in infected animals; findings published in Cell Host & Microbe.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Research is preliminary; no clinical trials or regulatory approvals reported. Findings suggest potential for a measles treatment for unvaccinated individuals, but efficacy and safety in humans remain untested.

analysis.brief_en: U.S. researchers have mapped the first comprehensive set of human antibodies against the measles virus, identifying a candidate antibody (4F09) that suppressed viral levels to undetectable in infected animals by locking the F protein and blocking cell entry. The NIH-funded team, led by Erica Ollmann Saphire at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology, used cryo-electron microscopy to resolve atomic-level interactions, challenging the prior assumption that protection relies solely on H-protein antibodies. Published in Cell Host & Microbe, the work points toward a potential therapeutic for individuals unable to receive vaccination amid rising global measles cases, though human trials have not yet been initiated.

news.source_body_en: U.S. researchers have mapped the first comprehensive set of human antibodies against the measles virus, identifying a candidate antibody (4F09) that suppressed viral levels to undetectable in infected animals by locking the F protein and blocking cell entry. The NIH-funded team, led by Erica Ollmann Saphire at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology, used cryo-electron microscopy to resolve atomic-level interactions, challenging the prior assumption that protection relies solely on H-protein antibodies. Published in Cell Host & Microbe, the work points toward a potential therapeutic for individuals unable to receive vaccination amid rising global measles cases, though human trials have not yet been initiated.
news.content_zh: 美国研究人员绘制了第一组针对 麻疹病毒 的全面人类抗体,确定了一种候选抗体 (4F09),该抗体通过锁定 F 蛋白并阻止细胞进入,将受感染动物中的病毒水平抑制至检测不到。NIH 资助的团队由拉霍亚免疫学研究所的 Erica Ollmann Saphire 领导,使用冷冻电子显微镜来解决原子级相互作用,挑战了之前的假设,即保护仅依赖于 H 蛋白抗体。该研究发表在《Cell 宿主 & Microbe》杂志上,指出了一种潜在的治疗方法,可以治疗在全球 麻疹 病例不断增加的情况下无法接受 疫苗接种 治疗的个体,尽管人体试验尚未启动。

Finch Walker USA TODAY NETWORK Updated Aug. 12, 2026, 1:48 p.m. ET Hear this story BETA DeeperDive is a GenAI Answer Engine built for trusted publishers. It delivers clear answers and real-time content based on what people are reading now — showcasing various stories from the USA TODAY Network that highlight not just what happened, but why it matters. Please reference surfaced articles to validate AI summary Explore DeeperDive Ask USA TODAY anything President Trump recently issued an executive order regarding the administration of the MMR vaccine. Vaccination rates for kindergarteners in Allegheny County have steadily declined over the past several years. Health officials urge parents to vaccinate their children as measles cases climb in Pennsylvania. President Donald Trump just issued an executive order on how the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine should be administered to children. Measles, which was eliminated from the United States in 2000, has seen a resurgence as vaccination rates have declined. And as parents prep to send their kids back to school, cases are climbing in Pennsylvania, according to state data. While Allegheny County has no reported cases of measles, health officials are urging parents to vaccinate their children against the disease before they head back to the classroom later this month. Here's what to know about vaccination rates in schools throughout the county. Pittsburgh area school vaccination rates During the 2025-2026 school year, 93.8% of all students in Allegheny County were fully vaccinated, according to a report from the county's health department. Among the unvaccinated, 0.4% had medical exemptions, 2.2% had religious exemptions and 1.6% had moral/philosophical exemptions, while 1.4% were noncompliant but still attending school. Trending beyond this story Hurricane Forecast Kennedy Center Luigi Mangione NBA Schedule The percentage of kids entering kindergarten fully vaccinated was lower than the overall rate, with only 91.8% of students in that age range coming to school with all required vaccines. That population did not exceed 95% for any required vaccine except hepatitis B. Here's a breakdown of the percentage of kindergarteners who were fully vaccinated: MMR: 93.8% Varicella-Zoster Virus: 92.9% Hepatitis B Virus: 95.1% Polio: 93.5% DTaP: 93.7% Private/independent and public schools had higher rates of vaccinations among kindergarteners (above 93% for all vaccines), while religious schools saw the lowest rates of vaccinations, with no rates above 90% for all vaccines. Overall, 60.5% of schools had a student population that was at least 95% fully vaccinated, with public schools reporting the highest percentage of these schools at 69.6%, followed by private/independent schools, then charter schools. Religious schools had the lowest percentage at just 31.4%. Have student vaccination rates declined in Pittsburgh? When more than 95% of a community is vaccinated against measles, that community has achieved herd immunity, meaning most people are protected against the disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control. Kindergarteners in Allegheny County have been below that threshold for several years, according to state records. Here's how overall vaccination rates have dropped among kindergarteners in Allegheny County: 2025-2026: 93.8% 2024-2025: 94.1% 2023-2024: 94.4% 2022-2023: 94.8% 2021-2022: 95.7% 2020-2021: 96.7% How many cases of measles have there been in Pennsylvania, US this year? There have been 232 reported cases of measles in Pennsylvania as of Aug. 10, when the most recent update to Pennsylvania Department of Health's dashboard happened. Thirty-eight people have been hospitalized. All cases were among people who were not fully vaccinated. Nationwide, there were 2,465 confirmed cases of measles, according to the CDC. The agency noted that it was aware of probable measles cases but that unconfirmed cases were not included in its data. Ninety-three percent of those cases occurred in people who were unvaccinated or who had an unknown vaccination status. Meanwhile, 3% of people with measles had received one MMR dose, while 4% were fully vaccinated. Nearly half of cases (1,189 or 48%) were among people age 5 to 19. How well does measles vaccine protect against infection, hospitalization, death? Two doses of the MMR vaccine provide 97% protection against the virus, according to the CDC, with children usually receiving their first dose at 12 to 15 months and a second at four to six years. It's estimated that one in five people who aren't vaccinated and get measles will need to be hospitalized, according to the CDC. Health experts have emphasized that the best protection against the disease is the vaccine, which can be given by itself, as part of an MMR vaccine or as part of the measles-mumps-rubella-varicella (MMRV) shot. How does measles spread? Measles is an airborne disease, which means that it spreads when an infected person exhales, coughs or sneezes, according to the World Health Organization. It can remain in the air for two hours after the infected person has left the area, and droplets can remain infectious on surfaces. A person with measles is contagious four days before the development of a rash to four days after the rash erupts, according to the WHO. What are the symptoms of measles? Signs of a measles infection generally appear seven to 14 days after someone encounters the virus. The following symptoms may be observed, according to the CDC: High fever Cough Runny nose Red, watery eyes Koplik spots (white spots inside the mouth) Rash that generally appears three to five days after the first symptoms, beginning as flat red spots on the face and hairline before spreading downward on the body Some people develop complications from measles. Complications may include: Ear infection Diarrhea Hospitalization Pneumonia Encephalitis, which can lead to convulsions, deafness or intellectual disability Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a fatal disease of the nervous system Death Pregnancy complications, which may include premature birth or a low-birth-weight baby A Billionaire's Reading List: 5 Books Cuban Says Everyone Should KnowCuban reads for three hours every morning. news.content_title: Confirmed measles case in Knox County
news.content: MOUNT VERNON — A laboratory-confirmed case of measles was identified on Aug. 3 in a resident residing in Knox County. The case has completed its isolation period. The Ohio Department of Health is working with Knox Public Health (KPH) to follow up on potential exposures and promote opportunities for vaccination. Knox Public Health is also working with the individual and their healthcare provider to identify contacts. KPH will notify the contacts and provide guidance on quarantining. Measles is a highly contagious virus. Individuals infected with measles can spread it to others, even before they have symptoms. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in the air after an infected person leaves the room. Symptoms usually appear 7 to 14 days after a person comes in contact with the virus, but it can take as long as 21 days for symptoms to appear. Measles symptoms include high fever (may spike from 103° F to 105° F), cough, runny nose, pink/red, watery eyes, and a red/brown blotchy rash. The rash will appear on the face and then spread to the trunk and extremities. Rash and other symptoms usually subside in 7 to 9 days. According to ODH, about one out of every five people who get measles will be hospitalized. One out of every 1,000 people with measles will develop brain swelling due to infection (encephalitis) which may lead to brain damage. One to 3 out of 1,000 people with measles will die, even with the best care. Treatment recommendations The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends all children get two doses of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, starting with the first dose at 12 through 15 months of age and the second dose at 4 through 6 years of age. Anyone traveling internationally should be fully vaccinated before traveling. Infants 6-11 months old should get one dose of the MMR vaccine before travel, then should receive two additional doses after their first birthday. Older children, adolescents, and adults should receive one or two doses of MMR vaccine if they do not have evidence of immunity. If you have received two doses of the MMR vaccine, your chances of getting measles are very low. After two doses, the vaccine is 97% effective at preventing measles. Residents are encouraged to talk to their healthcare provider about vaccination if they are unvaccinated or do not know if they are vaccinated. The MMR vaccine is safe and effective with hundreds of millions of doses given. Contact your medical provider or Knox County Community Health Center at 740-399-8008 if you have questions about measles or the MMR vaccination or would like to schedule a vaccination appointment. If you have symptoms, stay home, avoid contact with others, and call your healthcare provider. Do not show up in the waiting room without contacting the staff first in case you are contagious. For more information and updates, visit Knox Public Health’s website

(KATU) — Oregon reached 45 known measles cases this week as of Wednesday, surpassing 2024's peak of 31 cases. The state has not seen this many measles cases since a 1991 spike, when it recorded 100 cases. In 2025, the state had only one case. The increase comes amid a statewide decline in the rate of measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccinations. Currently, only 88% of Oregon's 2-year-olds have received an MMR vaccine. The national average is 90% to 91%. "We've seen several years of declining vaccination rates that really have been going on for about the last decade. As we went into the pandemic, we saw kind of a plateauing of that, but as we came out of the pandemic, we saw more parents and choosing not to fully vaccinate their children with the MMR, or measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, as well as other vaccines," said Dean Sidelinger, epidemiologist for the state of Oregon. READ ALSO | West Coast Health Alliance sticks with pediatric vaccine schedules despite Trump order The spike in new measles cases is occurring across the nation. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), there were 85 cases nationwide in 2000. So far this year, there have been 2,465 cases. Powered By 10 Sec Oregon measles cases hit highest level in decades as vaccination rates fall Next Stay Oregon has a higher per capita rate of measles cases than other Western states such as Washington and California. Oregon's rate has reached one case per 100,000 people, compared with 0.6 per 100,000 in Washington and 0.1 per 100,000 in California. Many other states with high case counts are Republican-leaning states. For example, Utah has recorded 524 cases this year, South Carolina has recorded 670 and Texas has recorded 190. According to the CDC, measles affects the respiratory system first before spreading throughout the body, causing high fever, cough, runny nose, red, watery eyes and a distinct rash. It can lead to severe illness or hospitalization, especially in young children and people with weakened immune systems. According to the National Foundation for Infectious Diseases: About 1 in 5 unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles will be hospitalized. The risk is higher in children younger than 5. One out of every 1,000 people with measles will develop brain swelling, which could lead to brain damage. As many as 1 in 20 children with measles will get pneumonia. One to three out of every 1,000 people with measles will die, even with the best care. According to the CDC, people who have received both doses of the MMR vaccine have only a 3% chance of contracting the disease if exposed. The MMR vaccine is less effective in people who are immunocompromised and children younger than 1, which is why health officials recommend the first MMR vaccine for children 12 months or older so it can be more effective. Measles can be much more dangerous for both groups if contracted. However, Sidelinger noted that because Oregon is currently experiencing a measles outbreak, parents of children 6 months or older can consult their pediatrician about giving their child the first MMR shot early to provide an extra layer of protection. If a child receives the first shot before turning 12 months old, a second shot is recommended at the 1-year mark for lifelong immunity. On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google OHIO (WOIO) - As of Thursday, the Ohio measles outbreak has grown to 69 confirmed cases so far this year, according to the state’s infectious disease dashboard. In July, the number of measles cases in the U.S. surpassed the tally for all of 2025. Ohio has now done the same, with cases trending up from the 45 confirmed last week. The state had 45 measles cases in 2025, seven cases in 2024 and one case in 2023. Here is the latest data for Ohio in 2026. County Name Number of Cases Ashtabula 17 Cuyahoga 3 Franklin 7 Geauga 16 Holmes 2 Knox 1 Ottawa 1 Trumbull 2 Tuscarawas 8 Wayne 2 Unknown 7 Those with measles have ranged in age from an infant to 40 years old. Five of the 45 infected individuals had to be hospitalized, according to the dashboard. As far as the recent surge, health experts are pointing to exposure events in Sugarcreek and Bloomfield. The Ashtabula County Health Department first reported two cases of measles back on July 23. Since then, local and state health departments continue working to identify and notify anyone who may have been exposed. People who have weakened immune systems may take longer to experience symptoms. According to experts, anyone seeking testing should contact their healthcare provider. You should not arrive at a healthcare facility without calling ahead if measles is suspected. Measles are preventable through vaccines and have been considered eliminated from the U.S. since 2000. In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status. Here are tips on how to spot symptoms of measles and how to protect yourself, from the Ohio Department of Health: Measles is extremely contagious and can spread to others through coughing and sneezing. It can be brought into Ohio by individuals who travel to places where measles is spreading. If people are not protected against the disease, nine out of 10 people who are exposed will become ill. The measles vaccine (called MMR as it protects against measles, mumps and rubella) is safe and effective at preventing measles. Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is extremely low. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before through four days after a rash appears. Measles symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite, and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts 5-6 days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications may also occur. Complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in youth. Copyright 2026 WOIO. analysis.time: As of Thursday, August 13, 2026, with cases trending up from the 45 confirmed last week. The outbreak has been ongoing since at least July 23, 2026, when the first two cases were reported.

analysis.event: Ohio reports 69 confirmed measles cases as of August 13, 2026, according to the state’s infectious disease dashboard. Health experts attribute the recent surge to exposure events in Sugarcreek and Bloomfield. Five of the 45 infected individuals had to be hospitalized.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak has surpassed the total number of cases in 2025, with 69 confirmed cases in 2026. The measles virus is extremely contagious, spreading through coughing and sneezing, and can remain infectious in the air for up to two hours. Complications are more common among children under 5, adults over 20, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals. analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Local and state health departments are actively working to identify and notify individuals who may have been exposed. The state is monitoring the outbreak and will participate in international discussions in November to assess measles-free status.

elements_zh.time: 截至 2026 年 8 月 13 日星期四,确诊病例较上周确诊的 45 例呈上升趋势。暴发 至少自 2026 年 7 月 23 日报告前两例病例以来一直在进行。
elements_zh.location_and_population: 美国俄亥俄州,病例分布在多个县,包括阿什塔比拉、凯霍加、富兰克林、吉奥加、霍姆斯、诺克斯、渥太华、特朗布尔、塔斯卡瓦斯、韦恩和未知。受影响人群的年龄范围从婴儿到40岁。
elements_zh.event: 根据俄亥俄州传染病仪表板,截至 2026 年 8 月 13 日,俄亥俄州报告有 69 例 麻疹 确诊病例。健康专家将最近的病例激增归因于 Sugarcreek 和 Bloomfield 的暴露事件。45 名感染者中有 5 人必须住院治疗。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 麻疹病毒 已超过 2025 年的病例总数,2026 年确诊病例为 69 例。麻疹病毒 传染性极强,通过咳嗽和打喷嚏传播,可在空气中保持传染性长达两个小时。并发症在 5 岁以下儿童、20 岁以上成人、孕妇和免疫功能低下的个体中更为常见。麻疹 疫苗(MMR)安全有效,两剂有效率达97%。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 地方和州卫生部门正在积极努力识别并通知可能接触过病毒的个人。健康专家建议,如果怀疑存在 麻疹,请联系医疗保健提供者进行检测,并避免前往医疗机构,无需事先通知。该州正在监控 麻疹 并将于 11 月参加国际讨论,以评估 麻疹 的无状态。

analysis_zh.location_and_population: 美国俄亥俄州,病例分布在多个县,包括阿什塔比拉、凯霍加、富兰克林、吉奥加、霍姆斯、诺克斯、渥太华、特朗布尔、塔斯卡瓦斯、韦恩和未知。受影响人群的年龄范围从婴儿到40岁。
analysis_zh.event: 根据俄亥俄州传染病仪表板,截至 2026 年 8 月 13 日,俄亥俄州报告有 69 例 麻疹 确诊病例。健康专家将最近的病例激增归因于 Sugarcreek 和 Bloomfield 的暴露事件。45 名感染者中有 5 人必须住院治疗。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 麻疹病毒 已超过 2025 年的病例总数,2026 年确诊病例为 69 例。麻疹病毒 传染性极强,通过咳嗽和打喷嚏传播,可在空气中保持传染性长达两个小时。并发症在 5 岁以下儿童、20 岁以上成人、孕妇和免疫功能低下的个体中更为常见。麻疹 疫苗(MMR)安全有效,两剂有效率达97%。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 地方和州卫生部门正在积极努力识别并通知可能接触过病毒的个人。健康专家建议,如果怀疑存在 麻疹,请联系医疗保健提供者进行检测,并避免前往医疗机构,无需事先通知。该州正在监控 麻疹 并将于 11 月参加国际讨论,以评估 麻疹 的无状态。

Early symptoms of measles include high fever, cough, runny nose and red/watery eyes. Those symptoms can start eight to 12 days after exposure. Arts & Entertainment Santa Barbara Live Music Venues Living Food & Drink Opinion Events Sports Obituaries Real Estate Indy Parenting Cover Stories Wedding Santa Barbara Green Guide Classifieds Advertise About Us Contact Us Create Event Subscribe News Health Santa Barbara County Reports First Measles Case Since 2019 Public Health Confirms Person Who Recently Returned from International Travel Has Come Down with Virus By Jean Yamamura Tue Aug 11, 2026 | 5:55pm Share this: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on X (Opens in new window) X Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Print (Opens in new window) Print Add independent.com on Google Add the SB Independent as your preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Credit: Courtesy The measles has been steadily making its way toward Santa Barbara and arrived this week. County Public Health confirmed Monday that a person who’d recently returned from international travel came down with the virus. The department is in infection control mode and coordinating with healthcare providers over potential exposure. They could not state where in the county the patient resided for privacy reasons, said spokesperson Jessica Martinez. In the recent nationwide outbreak, Ventura County confirmed one case of measles earlier this month and another was reported in San Luis Obispo in December 2025. Santa Barbara had a transient finding of measles virus in its wastewater in September 2025, but it was just once. news.content_title: New measles case confirmed in Clark County, bringing year’s total to 17
news.content: Clark County Public Health has confirmed a new case of measles in the county, the agency announced Tuesday. A child tested positive after being seen at AFC Urgent Care Camas at 180 N.E. 192nd Ave., while they were contagious. People who were at the clinic from 2 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. Friday may have been exposed. People who were at the clinic at that time, have not been vaccinated against measles or have not had measles in the past are at risk for getting sick and should stay home and out of public places for 21 days, Public Health said. During that time, anyone who believes they have symptoms of measles should call their healthcare provider before visiting the medical office to make a plan that avoids exposing others. So far this year, Clark County has had 17 cases of measles. Seven cases were reported in January , one in February and eight in July . Fifteen of the 17 cases involved unvaccinated children; the vaccination statuses of two adult cases were unknown. Measles is a highly contagious and potentially serious illness caused by a virus. The virus spreads through the air after a person with measles coughs or sneezes. A person with measles can spread the virus before they show symptoms, and the virus can linger in the air after someone who is infectious has left. Measles symptoms begin with a fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, followed by a rash that usually starts on the head and spreads to the rest of the body. A person exposed to measles will begin to get sick about one to three weeks after exposure. People are contagious up to four days before and after the rash appears. Public Health urges people who are not protected against measles to get vaccinated. Residents who have questions about the vaccine or are unsure whether they are protected should talk to their healthcare provider. Vaccination records are also available through the state’s MyIR Mobile system. Measles poses the highest risk to people who have not been vaccinated, including infants younger than 12 months. The MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine provides the best protection against measles. One dose of the vaccine is about 93 percent effective at preventing measles. Two doses are about 97 percent effective. Measles can be serious for all age groups. However, children younger than 5 and adults older than 20 are more likely to suffer from measles complications. The U.S. has hit a 35-year high in measles cases with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reporting 2,465 confirmed cases as of Aug. 6. news.content: Skip to main content The Mirror US - News, Sports, Celebrities and Showbiz News Sports Entertainment Lifestyle More News US News Politics Weather World News Royals Health Science Weird News Entertainment Celebrity News TV Movies Music Money Tech Tech News Travel Sports NFL NBA WNBA Soccer Golf MLB Tennis Boxing F1 MMA NHL Other Sports Lifestyle Food & Drink Parenting Dating & Relationships Shopping Fitness Fashion & Beauty Gardening Horoscopes Check out our editions: UK US ES-US IRE CLOSE Donald Trump US News Entertainment Sports About Us All Out Soccer Newsletter Signup Check out our editions: UK US ES-US IRE News US News Politics Weather World News Royals Health Science Weird News Entertainment Celebrity News TV Movies Music Money Tech Tech News Travel Sports NFL NBA WNBA Soccer Golf MLB Tennis Boxing F1 MMA NHL Other Sports Lifestyle Food & Drink Parenting Dating & Relationships Shopping Fitness Fashion & Beauty Gardening Horoscopes Donald Trump US News Entertainment Sports About Us All Out Soccer Newsletter Signup ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ News US News Donald Trump Donald Trump boasts that flu vaccine is no longer recommended for kids as measles cases soar The president has long questioned the safety of MMR immunizations, despite numerous studies showing no link between dosing and autism News Mataeo Smith News Reporter 22:15 ET, 11 Aug 2026 View 4 Images The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) currently recommends 18 childhood vaccinations(Image: AFP via Getty Images) President Donald Trump bragged about gutting flu and other vaccine mandates for children as the United States sees the highest number of measles cases in more than three decades. Article continues below Undo The president has long questioned the safety of MMR immunizations, despite numerous studies showing no link between the doses and autism. His new policy has drawn criticism from medical experts, who claim it could lower vaccination rates and expose kids to dangerous infections. Nevertheless, Trump touted his policy. Article continues below "Very importantly, vaccinations for hepatitis B, COVID-19, and influenza, among others, are no longer recommended for all children. In addition, this executive order directs the attorney general to advance legal challenges against states that violate children's rights to religious or medical vaccinations," he said. READ MORE: 24-hour flu advice rolled out as hospital admissions climb by 9% READ MORE: ABC David Muir fans say 'we're screwed' as host drops terrifying update The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) currently recommends 18 childhood vaccinations, but the order suggests reducing that number to 11. Trump’s order is more guidance than command — school vaccine requirements are decided by individual states, not the federal government. The order recommends a long list of routine childhood vaccines, including measles, mumps, and rubella, as well as protection against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, Hib, pneumococcal disease, HPV, and chickenpox. The Rest Report | SponsoredSponsored Why Your Morning Dizziness Won't Go Away (What Most Doctors Miss) Undo Forbes | SponsoredSponsored Mechanics Agree: If Your Car Is Out Of Warranty Do This Undo View 4 Images The number of measles cases in the U.S. has reached a 35-year high(Image: AFP via Getty Images) "We're reducing them," Trump said. "It's not only that you're doing fewer vaccines, or jabs, as they say, but you're doing them in a series of visits to the doctor." The MMR vaccine might be "quite lethal" if administered all at once, according to the president. He likened it to injecting a child's body with a bottle of Pepsi. A single dose of MMR is 0.5 ml, according to the FDA. View 4 Images A panel is scheduled to determine in November whether the U.S. will still be considered to have eradicated measles(Image: AFP via Getty Images) In response to a reporter's request for proof of the "lethal" assertion, Trump stated, "What I've heard is that there are some people that say it is that way." According to recent data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the number of measles cases in the U.S. has reached a 35-year high. Just seven months into 2026, there have been 2,318 confirmed cases of measles in the nation, up from a high of 2,289 instances the previous year, when two unvaccinated children died from the illness. Click here to follow the Mirror US on Google News to stay up to date with all the latest news, sports, and entertainment stories View 4 Images More cases of measles have been reported in the U.S. in the last 18 months than in the previous 25 years(Image: AFP via Getty Images) The U.S. has seen a rise in vaccine hesitancy in recent years, resulting in lower immunization rates and more cases. Article continues below A panel is scheduled to determine in November whether the U.S. will still be considered to have eradicated measles, a status that Canada lost last year. After a year or more of sustained transmission of the same measles virus strain, a nation risks losing its eradication status. More cases of measles have been reported in the U.S. in the last 18 months than in the previous 25 years. ENJOYED THIS STORY? Actions Facebook Tweet Email Utah has the nation’s highest measles rate, following years of declining vaccination Prev Next By: Max Roth Posted 11:22 PM, Aug 11, 2026 and last updated 11:54 PM, Aug 11, 2026 SALT LAKE CITY — Utah is the worst state in the country for measles cases per capita, and the numbers behind that distinction reveal how dramatically the state's vaccination landscape has shifted over the past 15 years. Nationally, there have been 2,465 measles cases so far this year. Utah and South Carolina together account for 48% of those cases. On a per-capita basis, Utah is the nation's hottest hot spot for measles outbreaks. WATCH: Students mix measles outbreak with a return to Utah classrooms Students mix measles outbreak with a return to Utah classrooms The state's vaccination rate tells a significant part of the story. In 2009 and 2010, Utah had the seventh-highest kindergarten vaccination rate in the nation at 97.7%. Last year, that rate had fallen to 88.6%, ranking Utah 43rd in the country — the third-biggest decline in vaccination rates of any state over that period. That matters because measles requires 95% vaccination coverage to achieve herd immunity. Utah is now well below that threshold. The outbreak is concentrated in three health districts: the Tri County District of eastern Utah, the Central Utah Health District, and the Southwest District. Those districts represent 12% of Utah's population but account for 64% of the state's measles cases. In those rural outbreak districts, one in every 1,000 people has already caught measles during this outbreak. On the Wasatch Front, that figure is one in 13,000. Measles by the numbers in Utah: Measles by the numbers in Utah Vaccination status is a defining factor in individual risk. Of unvaccinated Utahns, about one in every 440 has caught measles. For vaccinated Utahns, that figure drops to approximately one in every 47,000. In total, 617 unvaccinated Utahns have gotten measles in the last two years while 68 vaccinated Utahns have been confirmed with the disease. In 30 cases, vaccination status is unknown. The state counts someone as vaccinated if they've gotten one or more shots, though guidelines recommend getting two. analysis.brief_en: A measles case has been confirmed in western Kentucky, with health officials suspecting an outbreak. The report, published by Louisville Public Media on August 14, 2026, highlights the presence of the measles virus in the region. While the confirmation of a single case is noted, no further details on the number of cases, deaths, or specific containment measures are provided. The report indicates that health officials are monitoring the situation closely, but the evidence does not specify the extent of the outbreak or the risk level. This information is crucial for public health awareness and response planning in the area.

news.title_zh: 肯塔基州西部确诊 麻疹 病例,卫生官员怀疑 麻疹 - 路易斯维尔公共媒体
news.source_body_en: A measles case has been confirmed in western Kentucky, with health officials suspecting an outbreak. The report, published by Louisville Public Media on August 14, 2026, highlights the presence of the measles virus in the region. While the confirmation of a single case is noted, no further details on the number of cases, deaths, or specific containment measures are provided. The report indicates that health officials are monitoring the situation closely, but the evidence does not specify the extent of the outbreak or the risk level. This information is crucial for public health awareness and response planning in the area.
news.content_zh: 肯塔基州西部已确诊一例 麻疹 病例,卫生官员怀疑是 麻疹 病例。该报告由路易斯维尔公共媒体于 2026 年 8 月 14 日发布,强调了 麻疹病毒 在该地区的存在。虽然注意到了单个病例的确认,但没有提供有关病例数、死亡人数或具体遏制措施的进一步细节。报告指出,卫生官员正在密切监测局势,但证据并未具体说明 暴发 的范围或风险级别。这些信息对于该地区的公共卫生意识和应对计划至关重要。

news.content: Skip to main content 89.9 FM Live From The University Of New Mexico Public Health New Mexico New measles exposure in Artesia KUNM | By Daniel Montaño Published August 13, 2026 at 4:32 PM MDT Facebook Email Print Your browser doesn’t support HTML5 audio The measles, Mumps and Rubella vaccine is this best protection against measles according to state officials. An individual with measles, the 18th case in New Mexico so far this year, might have exposed members of the public to the virus from August 6 through August 11 in Artesia. Annie Rice The New Mexico Department of Health announced Thursday a new measles case has been confirmed in Eddy County in the Southeast, bringing the state's case count to 18 total in 2026. People may have been exposed to this new case at locations around Artesia during the second week of August. This newest case of measles was most likely acquired out-of-state, according to the DOH, with the individual not displaying symptoms until after arriving in New Mexico. news.content_title: As Pennsylvania measles cases grow, so do immunization rates, says DOH
news.content: Measles cases continue to grow in York and surrounding counties as many school districts around the commonwealth are beginning to start a new year. According to numbers released by the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) Wednesday, Aug. 12, York County has reported 14 cases of measles to the DOH since mid-June. There have been 66 cases reported around the state in the last seven days. Of the 258 cases reported around the state, 246 have come since April. More: Want a new pet? Free adoption events set at York County SPCA More: Rutter's eyes alcohol sales at southern York County convenience store The number of counties reporting at least one measles case has grown to 19. There were only three counties reporting measles cases for the first three months of 2026. Lancaster County continues to be the epicenter of the disease in Pennsylvania with 145. Of those, 137 have come since April. Nearby Chester County has had 24 cases reported since April. Adults between the ages of 18 and 49 have had the most reported cases of the disease. According to the DOH, 151 cases since April have been reported in that age group while cases among children 0 to 17 number 81 in the same period. While measles cases have grown, so have immunization numbers have grown in the last three months. Of the more than 2,700 immunizations administered by the DOH this year, 1,949 measles immunizations have been administered since June. >> Want to stay up to date on the latest news? Sign up for our newsletters. DOH spokesperson Neil Ruhland said that the best protection against getting the measles is getting immunized, and the majority of Pennsylvanians seem to be getting the message. “School-aged children in Pennsylvania have a high vaccination rate, with more than 93% of all kindergarteners being fully vaccinated against measles,” Ruhland said. “Since the majority of students are fully vaccinated, our schools benefit from robust community immunity that serves as a powerful barrier against the virus, so the risk of measles is low for Pennsylvania students as schools begin their fall classes.” Please consider subscribing to support local journalism. He said since the majority of students are fully vaccinated, Pennsylvania schools benefit from robust community immunity that serves as a powerful barrier against the virus. “So, the risk of measles is low for Pennsylvania students as schools begin their fall classes,” Ruhland said. Ruhland said, after two doses of the MMR vaccine, it provides 97% lifetime protection from contracting measles. Pharmacies inside Giant Food Stores are now offering the MMR vaccine. Go HERE to make an appointment at a store near you. The DOH launched a new dashboard Aug. 3 to show parents the immunization rates among kindergarten, seventh grade and 12th grade students on individual school campuses. The dashboard can be found at School Immunization Rates . Executive order decreases recommended immunizations Just as immunization numbers are beginning to grow in Pennsylvania ahead of school starting, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to change immunization rules. The executive order signed by the President Monday, Aug. 10 recommends all children get immunizations to provide protection for 11 diseases – a decrease from the 18 diseases recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in 2024. Immunizations no longer recommended for all children are now recommended for shared clinical decision-making, ensuring that parents have all options available to them. The executive order also recommends separating out the combined MMR vaccine, which is used to prevent the measles, into three single-disease shots and recommends administering all vaccines during separate medical visits to give parents more options regarding the timing and frequency of this vaccine administration. Gov. Josh Shapiro said on social media Monday in response to the executive order that Pennsylvania will continue to give public health guidance based on science and facts. “Once again, Donald Trump and (Department of Health and Human Services Secretary) RFK Jr. are screwing around with the childhood vaccine schedule — ignoring decades of science, sowing chaos and confusion, and spreading dangerous misinformation that put kids and families at risk,” Shapiro said. The state, Shapiro said, has already taken RFK Jr. to court to protect Pennsylvanians' freedom to make the best health care decisions for themselves and their kids. “Because here in Pennsylvania, we trust experts, doctors, and parents to make the best decisions for our families — not conspiracy theorists,” Shapiro said. news.content_original: Measles cases continue to grow in York and surrounding counties as many school districts around the commonwealth are beginning to start a new year. According to numbers released by the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) Wednesday, Aug. 12, York County has reported 14 cases of measles to the DOH since mid-June. There have been 66 cases reported around the state in the last seven days. Of the 258 cases reported around the state, 246 have come since April. More: Want a new pet? Free adoption events set at York County SPCA More: Rutter's eyes alcohol sales at southern York County convenience store The number of counties reporting at least one measles case has grown to 19. There were only three counties reporting measles cases for the first three months of 2026. Lancaster County continues to be the epicenter of the disease in Pennsylvania with 145. Of those, 137 have come since April. Nearby Chester County has had 24 cases reported since April. Adults between the ages of 18 and 49 have had the most reported cases of the disease. According to the DOH, 151 cases since April have been reported in that age group while cases among children 0 to 17 number 81 in the same period. While measles cases have grown, so have immunization numbers have grown in the last three months. Of the more than 2,700 immunizations administered by the DOH this year, 1,949 measles immunizations have been administered since June. >> Want to stay up to date on the latest news? Sign up for our newsletters. DOH spokesperson Neil Ruhland said that the best protection against getting the measles is getting immunized, and the majority of Pennsylvanians seem to be getting the message. “School-aged children in Pennsylvania have a high vaccination rate, with more than 93% of all kindergarteners being fully vaccinated against measles,” Ruhland said. “Since the majority of students are fully vaccinated, our schools benefit from robust community immunity that serves as a powerful barrier against the virus, so the risk of measles is low for Pennsylvania students as schools begin their fall classes.” Please consider subscribing to support local journalism. He said since the majority of students are fully vaccinated, Pennsylvania schools benefit from robust community immunity that serves as a powerful barrier against the virus. “So, the risk of measles is low for Pennsylvania students as schools begin their fall classes,” Ruhland said. Ruhland said, after two doses of the MMR vaccine, it provides 97% lifetime protection from contracting measles. Pharmacies inside Giant Food Stores are now offering the MMR vaccine. Go HERE to make an appointment at a store near you. The DOH launched a new dashboard Aug. 3 to show parents the immunization rates among kindergarten, seventh grade and 12th grade students on individual school campuses. The dashboard can be found at School Immunization Rates . Executive order decreases recommended immunizations Just as immunization numbers are beginning to grow in Pennsylvania ahead of school starting, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to change immunization rules. The executive order signed by the President Monday, Aug. 10 recommends all children get immunizations to provide protection for 11 diseases – a decrease from the 18 diseases recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in 2024. Immunizations no longer recommended for all children are now recommended for shared clinical decision-making, ensuring that parents have all options available to them. The executive order also recommends separating out the combined MMR vaccine, which is used to prevent the measles, into three single-disease shots and recommends administering all vaccines during separate medical visits to give parents more options regarding the timing and frequency of this vaccine administration. Gov. Josh Shapiro said on social media Monday in response to the executive order that Pennsylvania will continue to give public health guidance based on science and facts. “Once again, Donald Trump and (Department of Health and Human Services Secretary) RFK Jr. are screwing around with the childhood vaccine schedule — ignoring decades of science, sowing chaos and confusion, and spreading dangerous misinformation that put kids and families at risk,” Shapiro said. The state, Shapiro said, has already taken RFK Jr. to court to protect Pennsylvanians' freedom to make the best health care decisions for themselves and their kids. “Because here in Pennsylvania, we trust experts, doctors, and parents to make the best decisions for our families — not conspiracy theorists,” Shapiro said. York Daily Record reporter Meredith Willse contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on York Daily Record: As Pennsylvania measles cases grow, so do immunization rates, says DOH

Huntingdon County has logged its first case, marking the first appearance of measles in that jurisdiction this year. The surge contrasts sharply with prior years, when only 16 cases were recorded in 2025 and four in 2023. Health authorities continue to track and report cases, but the evidence does not specify active containment measures such as vaccination drives or contact tracing in the supplied report.

supplementary_news.content_title: As measles cases continue to surge, are Pittsburgh schools prepared?
supplementary_news.content: President Donald Trump just issued an executive order on how the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine should be administered to children. Measles, which was eliminated from the United States in 2000, has seen a resurgence as vaccination rates have declined . And as parents prep to send their kids back to school , cases are climbing in Pennsylvania, according to state data . While Allegheny County has no reported cases of measles, health officials are urging parents to vaccinate their children against the disease before they head back to the classroom later this month. Here's what to know about vaccination rates in schools throughout the county. Pittsburgh area school vaccination rates During the 2025-2026 school year, 93.8% of all students in Allegheny County were fully vaccinated, according to a report from the county's health department. Among the unvaccinated, 0.4% had medical exemptions, 2.2% had religious exemptions and 1.6% had moral/philosophical exemptions, while 1.4% were noncompliant but still attending school. Measles cases continue to grow, sparking debate among Americans on vaccines 1 of 11 Instructions for a Measles vaccination is seen outside of the Lubbock Public Health facility on April 9, 2025 in Lubbock, Texas. The city of Lubbock has confirmed a second measles related death amidst an ongoing outbreak which began in late January. As of early April, the Texas Department of State Health Services have confirmed over 500 cases, within 22 counties, ranging from the South Plains toward the Panhandle. (Brandon Bell, Getty Images) More The percentage of kids entering kindergarten fully vaccinated was lower than the overall rate, with only 91.8% of students in that age range coming to school with all required vaccines. That population did not exceed 95% for any required vaccine except hepatitis B. Here's a breakdown of the percentage of kindergarteners who were fully vaccinated: Varicella-Zoster Virus: 92.9% Private/independent and public schools had higher rates of vaccinations among kindergarteners (above 93% for all vaccines), while religious schools saw the lowest rates of vaccinations, with no rates above 90% for all vaccines. Overall, 60.5% of schools had a student population that was at least 95% fully vaccinated, with public schools reporting the highest percentage of these schools at 69.6%, followed by private/independent schools, then charter schools. Religious schools had the lowest percentage at just 31.4%. Have student vaccination rates declined in Pittsburgh? When more than 95% of a community is vaccinated against measles, that community has achieved herd immunity, meaning most people are protected against the disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control . Kindergarteners in Allegheny County have been below that threshold for several years, according to state records . Here's how overall vaccination rates have dropped among kindergarteners in Allegheny County: How many cases of measles have there been in Pennsylvania, US this year? There have been 232 reported cases of measles in Pennsylvania as of Aug. 10, when the most recent update to Pennsylvania Department of Health's dashboard happened. Thirty-eight people have been hospitalized. All cases were among people who were not fully vaccinated. Nationwide, there were 2,465 confirmed cases of measles, according to the CDC . The agency noted that it was aware of probable measles cases but that unconfirmed cases were not included in its data. Ninety-three percent of those cases occurred in people who were unvaccinated or who had an unknown vaccination status. Meanwhile, 3% of people with measles had received one MMR dose, while 4% were fully vaccinated. Nearly half of cases (1,189 or 48%) were among people age 5 to 19. How well does measles vaccine protect against infection, hospitalization, death? Two doses of the MMR vaccine provide 97% protection against the virus, according to the CDC , with children usually receiving their first dose at 12 to 15 months and a second at four to six years. It's estimated that one in five people who aren't vaccinated and get measles will need to be hospitalized, according to the CDC. Health experts have emphasized that the best protection against the disease is the vaccine, which can be given by itself, as part of an MMR vaccine or as part of the measles-mumps-rubella-varicella (MMRV) shot. How does measles spread? Measles is an airborne disease, which means that it spreads when an infected person exhales, coughs or sneezes, according to the World Health Organization . It can remain in the air for two hours after the infected person has left the area, and droplets can remain infectious on surfaces. A person with measles is contagious four days before the development of a rash to four days after the rash erupts, according to the WHO . What are the symptoms of measles? Signs of a measles infection generally appear seven to 14 days after someone encounters the virus. The following symptoms may be observed, according to the CDC : Koplik spots (white spots inside the mouth) Rash that generally appears three to five days after the first symptoms, beginning as flat red spots on the face and hairline before spreading downward on the body Some people develop complications from measles. Complications may include: Encephalitis, which can lead to convulsions, deafness or intellectual disability Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a fatal disease of the nervous system Pregnancy complications, which may include premature birth or a low-birth-weight baby This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: As measles cases continue to surge, are Pittsburgh schools prepared?

supplementary_news.content_title: Ohio measles outbreak cases rise again, surpass last year's numbers
supplementary_news.content: News Sports Business Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE Ohio measles outbreak cases rise again, surpass last year's numbers Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Aug. 13, 2026, 3:17 p.m. ET Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues to grow, spreading to another county and surpassing the total number of cases from 2025 at the last count. Harrison County Public Health reported a measles case there on Aug. 12. Statewide, the Ohio Department of Health is reporting 69 cases in 11 counties, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Aug. 13. That's up from 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Nationwide, measles cases nationwide hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released July 22 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 2,295 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio; counties reporting cases Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashtabula: 17 Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 7 Geauga: 16 Harrison: 3 Holmes: 2 Knox: 1 Ottawa: 1 Trumbull: 2 Tuscarawas: 8 Wayne: 2 Unknown: 7 The latest case count reflects two previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with 45 in 2025, seven cases in 2024 and one case in 2023. Where are measles cases spreading? While Harrison County Public Health reported one case of measles as of Aug. 7, the state dashboard shows two additional cases there. The Wayne County Health Department reports some of its cases are likely associated with a previously identified measles exposure event at Smokey Lane Stables, 686 Smokey Lane Road NW in Sugarcreek, on July 17. One of the Tuscarawas cases is from the same event, that health department reports. Geauga Public Health reports that the individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. In Trumbull County, health officials report that infected individuals were at the Walmart in Liberty on July 29 and Akron Children's Mahoning Valley Emergency Department in Boardman on Aug. 2, during the time they were able to spread the virus. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Why are measles cases on the rise? Ohio vaccination rates Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventives, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine ahead of back-to-school season. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023, the most recent year available from ODH. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, USA TODAY reports. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. Featured Weekly Ad

supplementary_news.content: News Sports Business Data Real Estate Obituaries eNewspaper Legals PUBLIC SAFETY One case of measles confirmed in Tioga County Jillian McCarthy Binghamton Press & Sun Bulletin Updated Aug. 14, 2026, 12:06 p.m. ET One case of measles has been confirmed in Tioga County. In a statement on Aug. 14, Tioga County Public Health announced an investigation into one confirmed case of measles in an unvaccinated county resident. Measles, a viral illness spread through coughing and sneezing, can remain alive and infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person has left the room, according to county public health. As part of the investigation, county public health officials are conducting contact tracing. They have successfully identified and are directly contacting all individuals known to have been exposed. An individual who has measles is contagious four days prior to a rash beginning and four days after the rash appears. Symptoms of measles typically begin between seven and 14 days after exposure to the virus and nine out of 10 unvaccinated people who are exposed to the virus will contract it. So far in 2026, there have been six confirmed cases of measles in New York City and 12 elsewhere in New York for 18 total cases as of Aug. 14, according to the New York State Department of Health. How to stay safe The overall risk of measles to the general public remains low, particularly for individuals who are fully vaccinated against the disease, according to county public health. Measles, however, is extremely contagious, and anyone unvaccinated, pregnant, under 12 months of age or immunocompromised is at a higher risk and should talk with their health care provider. If you were exposed or you think you may have been exposed, it's recommended to monitor you and your family members for symptoms. Early symptoms will typically appear between seven and 14 days after exposure and can include a high fever, often rising to about 101 degrees, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A red, blotchy rash typically appears three to five days after initial symptoms begin, usually starting on the face along the hairline and spreading downward to the rest of the body, according to the county public health. If you are seeking medical attention, do not walk into a clinic, urgent care or emergency room without calling ahead. Inform them that you may have been exposed to measles ahead of time — this allows health care facilities to take precautions such as placing you in an isolated room to prevent spreading the virus to other vulnerable patients in the waiting room or other areas. Tioga County Public Health is asking anyone with questions to call 607-687-8600 or visit ph.tiogacountyny.gov. One case of measles confirmed in Tioga County One case of measles has been confirmed in Tioga County. In a statement on Aug. 14, Tioga County Public Health announced an investigation into one confirmed case of measles in an unvaccinated county resident. Measles, a viral illness spread through coughing and sneezing, can remain alive and infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person has left the room, according to county public health. Advertisement Advertisement As part of the investigation, county public health officials are conducting contact tracing. They have successfully identified and are directly contacting all individuals known to have been exposed. An individual who has measles is contagious four days prior to a rash beginning and four days after the rash appears. Symptoms of measles typically begin between seven and 14 days after exposure to the virus and nine out of 10 unvaccinated people who are exposed to the virus will contract it. So far in 2026, there have been six confirmed cases of measles in New York City and 12 elsewhere in New York for 18 total cases as of Aug. 14, according to the New York State Department of Health. More: Meet two candidates running to become Tioga County sheriff How to stay safe The overall risk of measles to the general public remains low, particularly for individuals who are fully vaccinated against the disease, according to county public health. Measles, however, is extremely contagious, and anyone unvaccinated, pregnant, under 12 months of age or immunocompromised is at a higher risk and should talk with their health care provider. Advertisement Advertisement If you were exposed or you think you may have been exposed, it's recommended to monitor you and your family members for symptoms. Early symptoms will typically appear between seven and 14 days after exposure and can include a high fever, often rising to about 101 degrees, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A red, blotchy rash typically appears three to five days after initial symptoms begin, usually starting on the face along the hairline and spreading downward to the rest of the body, according to the county public health. If you are seeking medical attention, do not walk into a clinic, urgent care or emergency room without calling ahead. Inform them that you may have been exposed to measles ahead of time — this allows health care facilities to take precautions such as placing you in an isolated room to prevent spreading the virus to other vulnerable patients in the waiting room or other areas. Tioga County Public Health is asking anyone with questions to call 607-687-8600 or visit ph.tiogacountyny.gov.
